maintopic: REPORTED TRADE MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question of the Prime Minister. I notice that in the newspapers we are told a trade mission is proceeding to China. speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORTED TRADE MISSION TO COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I
could answer that question for the hon. member. There is no trade mission as such proceeding to China in the sense that a large group of people are going on a mission; nothing of that sort is taking place. The situation is simply this. For a number of years we have had a trade commissioner living in Hong Kong and looking after Canada's trade interests in that area. During the course of the summer his area was extended to include adjacent territory, and some time ago our department suggested to him that he might look into the possibilities of trade on the mainland. It was left to him to use his own initiative as to how he would go about that enterprise.
What is happening at the moment is that his proposal is to leave some time in early November for a period of perhaps two weeks. He may visit four cities in China: Peking,
Tientsin, Canton and Shanghai. What he will discover in the course of his visits I do not know. If there is a possibility of disposing of some of our good Canadian wheat in China, naturally he will report to us with regard to that. Actually, he is doing simply what the trade commissioner service throughout the world attempts to do, and that is initiate discussions with people who are interested in trade, discover possibilities for trade on the part of Canada, and inform Canadian businessmen as well as the Canadian government as to what the prospects are. It is a routine mission. It is not really a trade mission; it is just routine business, and it is just the initiative on the part of a trade commissioner dealing with the area that comes under his jurisdiction.

I wish to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce giving consideration to the licensing of off-site storage for grain at country points in order to ease congestion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. I have a reply here which deals with the situation as of last year and the present position. The licensing of off-site grain storage was the subject of discussions between the board of grain commissioners for Canada and the Canadian wheat board in June, 1956. At that time the two boards issued a press release and an instruction to handling companies which read as follows:
The licensing of off-site grain storage is a matter of concern to the board of grain commissioners for Canada and the Canadian wheat board. The board of grain commissioners are interested from the standpoint of actual licensing and the adequate warehousing of grain. The Canadian wheat board are interested from the standpoint of availability of grain for prompt shipment. Both boards have carefully reviewed their position in respect to the licensing of off-site storage facilities.
As a result of discussions between the two boards it has been decided that no further applications for off-site storage will be considered. This decision has been reached after careful consideration of the storage position, including the extent of off-site storage presently licensed and the immobility of grain stored in many types of off-site facilities.
As indicated by the statement at that time, the two boards were concerned about the volume of grain which was then being warehoused in off-site facilities. Should deterioration set in, there was no way in which this grain could be turned and there could never be assurance that grain in off-site facilities would be moved forward promptly for treatment in terminal elevators. Another factor was that off-site storage facilities were confined to certain delivery points, giving advantages that could not be extended to producers generally.
I have inquired from both the board of grain commissioners and the Canadian wheat board as to whether, in their opinion, any
Inquiries of the Ministry change should be made in the policy which was announced on June 25, 1956. Both boards are of the opinion that the present restriction on licensing of off-site storage should be continued. In their opinion off-site storage is not a solution to the congestion problem, and could result in serious problems in respect of grain stored in these immobile positions.

I wonder if I might ask a supplementary question. Would the minister make inquiries himself to see whether in fact grain in off-site storage is not just as mobile within a 24-hour period as grain in any elevator annex? Would he further make his own observations as to the quality of the grain in off-site storage, which I believe to be generally superior to the quality of the grain in present annexes, many of which are not up to standard?
I shall be glad to look into the question the hon. member has raised.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of his answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Acadia relative to offsite storage. Is it not a fact that the government is now approving and authorizing elevator companies to acquire off-site storage?
Mr. Speaker, I will have to take notice of that question.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: HOG CHOLERA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) asked several questions, as follows:
Has there been any importation of pork into Canada from the United States and, if so, in what form? Does the United States hog producer use live serum for the control of cholera in that country?
The answer is importations of pork into Canada from the United States in the first

six months of 1957 were as follows: Fresh pork, none; bacon, ham and other pork in prepared form, 160,548 pounds. All importations were cooked pork, in accordance with the provisions of a ministerial order prohibiting the importation of swine and uncooked pork into Canada.
In connection with the serum question, a live virus vaccine is used for the control of hog cholera in some states. I had perhaps better say in connection with that matter that anti-hog cholera serum, used widely in the United States in inoculating hogs against cholera, does not contain any virus, living or dead. Its effectiveness lies in its content of antibodies which protect against the disease.
Vaccines, also used in the control of hog cholera in the United States, are a totally different product from blood serums. Hog cholera vaccines contain the hog cholera virus itself and can be made with the virus either in live or attenuated form. I think that is what the hon. member was referring to rather than a serum.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with a question asked by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) relative to the prospective Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan and also questions that were asked by some other hon. members, I wish to advise that, subject to the approval of parliament, Canada will contribute $35 million to the Colombo plan in 1958.
For some years now the basic Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan has stood at $26.4 million. In order to meet certain additional expenditures in connection with the Warsak project in Pakistan and the Canada-India reactor, this amount was supplemented by a further $8 million both this year and last. We have now decided to do away with this idea of a basic contribution to which additional amounts are added. We shall therefore seek the authority of parliament to provide that the total vote for Canada's regular Colombo plan program be, as I stated a moment ago, $35 million for this year.
In connection with the expenditures being made thereunder we have agreed, first, to provide $1 million worth of flour to the government of Ceylon. The proceeds of the sale of this flour will be used by the government of Ceylon for various development projects.
Second, the government of Pakistan has drawn our attention to the very serious floods that occurred recently in west Pakistan and to the resulting need for food grains. We have therefore offered $2 million worth of wheat to the government of Pakistan out of Colombo plan funds and the government of Pakistan has indicated that this would be very welcome. This wheat will be shipped very shortly.
In India we have proposed to the government of that country that the balance of counterpart funds held by the Indian government which have been created by the sale of Canadian commodities supplied under the

Colombo plan will be used to meet the further rupee costs of the Canada-India reactor. These counterpart funds amount to the equivalent of $2,900,000.
In connection with other proposals concerning the Colombo plan program they will be announced in due course after they have been discussed with the governments concerned. Might I add that later today the leader of the Canadian delegation to the Colombo plan conference at Saigon, Hon. W. J. Browne, will be announcing in that country what I have stated here.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, October 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. R. Smith (Calgary South) for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to her speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Low.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I made a few remarks in French and in English, and then the inexorable hand of time indicated that it was almost ten o'clock, at which time the house kindly permitted me to resume my speech today.
(Translation):
Yesterday, most of my remarks were in French, but today I propose to speak in English, because I do not want the immediate effect of my words to be lost on the members of the government. That this should be the case is regrettable. However, in this loyal and friendly though earnest joust, no one will blame me for making use of the best weapons at my disposal.

The Address-Mr. Deniset
(Text):
Yesterday I was paying my compliments to one of Canada's great soldiers, and I still pay my respects today. However, I did advise the hon. gentleman that when I rose again it might be quite possible that I would disagree with him, and I find that it is my duty to bring to his full knowledge the great concern aroused throughout the country concerning government policy with regard to the militia. We know now that summer camps are not to be held in 1958. Militia personnel will have the opportunity to attend camps with the regular forces, but of course there will be fewer militia people interested because one of the great attractions of the militia is for one to train with his own unit.
Another loss could be from the point of view of teamwork. Teamwork is one of the fundamentals of sound military training. Furthermore the days of training have been reduced from 60 to 40 which means a total of 80 evenings of training. But if one excludes week-end schemes and range firing which should take at least five or six days of training the evenings of training will be reduced to about 68. In addition we now have the block syllabus based on civil defence precis taking 60 periods. This would mean at two periods an evening 30 evenings out of 68.
What does the department propose to do regarding recruit training, basic training, weapon training, qualifications for infantrymen, group 1, specialist training, signals training, driving and maintenance, qualification of N.C.O.'s, professional advancement training for officers, and so on? These are all questions that people across the country in the militia and people interested in the work of the militia are asking.
I must confess that at this stage I am a bit bewildered, and that many Canadians are bewildered. It is of the utmost necessity that the government determine what its policy is and, furthermore, state it clearly for the benefit of all.
I must turn now, Mr. Speaker, to some remarks which were made in this house by the Minister of National Defence. I refer to Hansard for Wednesday, October 16, at page 38. The minister was speaking of the militia, and I read what he is reported as having said:
That may not be as glamorous a role as some of the other ones which have in the past been carried out by the militia, but I am confident that the militia will render the same patriotic service in this role as it has always done, rather than seeking some phony, glamorous role which hardly exists.

It is true that the minister backtracked somewhat in his remarks, as is evident from what I shall read farther down on this page:
There is no suggestion of the militia having carried out in the past any role that could be considered as phony or glamorous, but there might be roles carried out in the future which would not be practical.
I feel it is possible that at that time the minister made a slip of the tongue, but I should like to have it placed on record that during the last three years I have had the privilege of commanding one of Canada's finest regiments, the Winnipeg Grenadiers. I relinquished that command at the end of September because of my obvious duties here in Ottawa. I will say this, that I do not consider the officers, non-commissioned officers or men under my command have performed any training during the last three years that could be termed either phony or impractical. We did not intend, during the winter training program, to contemplate any training that could be termed either phony or impractical.
Furthermore, I have been associated with the militia during the last eleven years, and I must say that neither the Winnipeg Grenadiers nor the 19 militia groups in greater Winnipeg have contemplated or carried out anything that could be termed either phony or impractical. I believe the same remarks will apply to the militia right across Canada. I feel that the thousands of Canadian people who have sacrificed so many evenings, so many week ends and so many vacations during the summer time, purely as a result of devotion to duty to carry out training with the militia, deserve an explanation, and I trust this explanation will be forthcoming sooner than in mere due course.
Another hon. gentleman on the front benches, Mr. Speaker, is one who has the job of selling wheat. He no doubt remembers the years we spent together at law school, and he can expect that we will resume the discussions that were started in those days. Following the example set by my leader, I do not propose to obstruct the minister's work, but certainly he can expect criticism, which I shall try to make as constructive as possible. The minister's task is so difficult and the difficulties facing Canadian agriculture are so great that I would rather help than engage in petty politics.
The agricultural problem in Canada is not new. It has been with us for many years, and is of such a nature that it is likely to remain with us for a great number of years. It cannot be solved in one day. As a matter of fact there are few solutions to the problem that could be said to be of a permanent nature

because of the economics involved. I have paid close attention to the many speeches that have been made, particularly by western members, concerning agriculture. Yesterday I found great enjoyment in listening to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson), and I want to congratulate him upon his speech. It definitely showed that he had done his home work. I would say that his remarks proved that the agricultural problem is indeed a very intricate one.
I was surprised, therefore, to hear the Prime Minister, in his address in reply to the speech from the throne, try to lay the blame on the previous administration. Surely he does not expect the Canadian people to be so naive as to believe him in that regard. He knows quite well that the previous administration did its best to try to retain markets and find new ones. He has the files at his disposal. The present government, after studying the matter with experts, created a committee of three wise men. They then sent four heavyweights to the United States for a conference on economic matters. What happened? The United States secretary of commerce is reported to have stated, "We fixed them." I do not believe that this is really what happened, but that is what was said.
These four heavyweights, including the Prime Minister, must have realized the tremendous difficulties, not only those that lie ahead but those which the previous administration had faced. Although I am a novice in this house, Mr. Speaker, I was surprised and saddened to hear a man as responsible as the Prime Minister of Canada trying to throw the blame for this situation on persons of whom it was never said they had been fixed, and when the present administration does not seem to be doing any better. It would appear that they are doing much worse. The people of Manitoba, at any rate, are not as gullible as the present government would like them to be.
We heard statements that there would be more trade with Great Britain and less with the United States. This interested the western farmer. It meant the possibility of greater sales of wheat and other grains. Then, when the British government proposed free trade between Britain and Canada, it was really humiliating to find the only reaction one of "intensive examination and consideration". It appeared as if Britain was calling Canada's bluff. I do not propose to say that at this time it is possible to implement complete free trade, although it is a goal of which we must not lose sight. There are, indeed, very formidable difficulties in the way. But why try to impress the western farmers by saying that free markets are to open in Britain; that wheat "galore" will be sold, and then
The Address-Mr. Deniset when there is a chance for the western farmer to sell his wheat the government admits that finding markets is not as easy as it would look on the surface. I might say, too, that one day the western farmers will call the Conservatives' bluff.
I should like to turn now to certain problems in my own constituency. I would point out that while these problems are local in their application, their solution will stem from government policy which has to be applied in many other constituencies across Canada. First of all I would refer to the matter of erosion. At the junction of the Assiniboine and Red rivers, in the very heart of the metropolitan area of greater Winnipeg, the combined waters of these rivers eats the earth away from the east bank of the Red river. This is where the St. Boniface hospital is situated, as well as many other buildings having a total value of well over $10 million. There is also Tache avenue, which is a main artery of the city of St. Boniface.
The situation thus created simply cannot be allowed to continue. I understand that some proposals were made to the government, but they are still under study. I noticed the statement made by the Minister of Public Works in which he said the federal government could not be held responsible for erosion unless it was attributable to navigation. I wonder what the government would do if the erosion was endangering navigation itself. The earth that is continually taken away from the bank falls into the river and lifts up its bed. Consequently it endangers navigation and, furthermore, increases the danger of floods. It is not necessary for me to recall to the house the anxious moments of the inhabitants of the Red river valley during the 1950 flood. In this regard I might add that the people of Manitoba are still very grateful for the assistance provided at that time. I shall leave this point now because I propose to take up the matter again with the Minister of Public Works.
Another problem in my constituency is caused by the fact that the town of Transcona used to be only a railway town practically under the control of the Canadian National Railways. Now it is a growing, prosperous and industrious community, the hub of southeastern Manitoba. The Canadian National Railways take the stand that they do not legally have to pay taxes to the municipality. All the town of Transcona gets is a grant in lieu of taxation. The town of Transcona is demanding that these grants be more realistic. Year after year resolutions are passed by meetings of mayors and municipalities asking for more realistic grants.

The Address-Mr. Deniset
There is also in Transcona the matter of getting the Canadian National Railways to pay their share of sewer and water installations on Pandora avenue, east of Madeline street. The railways have been asked to pay their share of these improvements but they refuse to do so, and their reason is that they feel that such sewers and water mains are of no useful purpose to them. This means that a municipal taxpayer who is close to the railways must pay more taxes than do other taxpayers.
It may very well be that the railways stand is solid on legal grounds. However, I am not speaking of the law at this time but rather of what would be a fair way in which to deal with taxpayers. One would expect that the Canadian National Railways could more easily afford to pay taxes than the small taxpayer. This again is a matter that I shall bring up again in the near future with the minister concerned.
I understand further that one line going through the municipality of Springfield does not pay anything, this again because of an old statute. One cannot but have a feeling at times that big people do not care about small people, many of them railway employees. Surely statutes do not exist solely to protect big people. Other statutes may be passed.
In conclusion I should like to set out the reasons why I do not propose to support the amendment to the amendment nor the amendment itself to the motion. I have first of all to look at the motion of the Social Credit party and I read as follows:
However, we regret that there is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that it is the government's intention to ask parliament to lay down a scientific, modem financial policy for Canada that will guide the Bank of Canada in its operations, . . .
The important governing words, I submit, are "scientific, modern financial policy". This would mean a scientific, modern financial policy according to Social Credit principles. I have read many articles about Social Credit and I have read a number of speeches made by Social Crediters, and as yet I must confess that I find their financial theories to be rather nebulous. Furthermore, their financial theories have not been applied in the two provinces which have Social Credit governments. I would venture to say that the success of the Social Credit party in these two provinces has been caused by the fairly sound administration by the people concerned, but it is in no way a proof that Social Credit principles are sound. For that reason I cannot support that particular amendment.

I now turn to the C.C.F. amendment, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to read the governing phrases:
We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house Your Majesty's advisers should give immediate consideration to the advisability of taking steps to deal with the menace of inflation, rapidly rising unemployment and other serious problems facing this country. We call upon the government to give immediate effect to the social and economic planning necessary to cope with these problems.
Here the governing word is "planning", and "planning" here can mean only planning a la C.C.F. I should now like to say a word about the C.C.F. I have followed their progress with great interest throughout the years, and I have found many admirable things in what they said. As a matter of fact, when they speak of social security and social justice I believe that they are preaching pure Liberal doctrine. I go along with them 100 per cent along those lines. I believe that the big must help the small and that the rich must help the poor. That is only charity, and that should be done.
On the other hand, when I follow their philosophy and principles to their logical and ultimate conclusion, I cannot but fear that we would end up with a form of bureaucratic government of the worst order. There is enough bureaucracy as it is. Too much government interference is not good. We would lose a sense of initiative and we would lose fundamental rights to private property and free enterprise. For these and other reasons I simply cannot go as far as they do. For that reason I cannot support their amendment.
Turning to the motion for the address itself, I should like to state that I do not propose to vote against the government on this occasion. The reason is simply this. My electors have asked me not to do so.

That statement applies not only to my electors but to the electors of the province of Manitoba. I am not speaking of parties right now; I am speaking of electors generally. In order to explain what I am talking about, let me refer to a certain statement that was made by the Prime Minister in his own speech. You will recall that he was asking us why we did not permit a vote to take place. Then pointing to the heckling he was receiving he said, "They have already jeered themselves out of this side of the house". It was a Shakespearean gesture. I cannot here re-enact the scene, Mr. Speaker, but at that time I could not help but think to myself, "If anything, the Conservatives have done nothing but promise their way out of this side of the house where I am".

I say this in all seriousness. Since the June 10 election I have been out in my own constituency and elsewhere in Manitoba. I have spoken to hundreds if not thousands of people. We talked about the election. We said, "What are we going to do now?" The most common remark was, "Well, we will see what they can do. They are in office. They promised many things, such as reduction of taxation and increases in services. Let us give them a fair chance but"- and it is that "but" that stands out-"watch out if it does not come true." Some even say, "Watch out when it becomes impossible". One cannot help but remember the old saying, Mr. Speaker: "You can fool some of the people all of the time, you can fool all the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time." Beware, I tell you-

speechtext:
As a new member, Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to congratulate you on your appointment to the high office you hold and to pledge my support in first learning the rules of this house and, second, in abiding by your rulings which I am sure will always be given in full sincerity.
May I next congratulate the mover (Mr. Smith) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the speech from the throne, which I feel they did excellently.
As the member representing the southern portion of the great northern city of Edmonton I am, of course, particularly interested in congratulating the member for Calgary South, our neighbouring southern city. As you know, out there normally we fight it out in football or anything else, but when we get here we have a rather close affinity. It is therefore, I feel, important that at this stage I agree with him on at least one question. He brought forward the question of the position of Canada's oil companies in comparison with American oil companies so far as income tax is concerned. I feel that it is fully justified that he should work within his party to achieve an improvement in this situation. Of course Calgary is the paper oil capital of
The Address-Mr. S. H. S. Thompson Canada and therefore it should be his duty to continue with this job. We in Edmonton have the production facilities.
I note that the hon. member who spoke immediately before me on behalf of the Liberal party took issue with our amendment to provide a scientific, modern, financial policy, on the basis that we had not already done so in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. May I remind him that the Liberal party proved through the courts that this was their responsibility at the federal level. I am very pleased to acknowledge the great compliment he paid our provincial administration in saying that what has been done has been accomplished through very sound administration.
In my opinion the importance of the memorable occasion which we witnessed at the opening of this parliament is not to be found only in the glorious traditions which were represented but rather the effectiveness displayed in the present and the good omens portended for the future. My wife and I were deeply conscious of the honour which had been given us when we had the privilege of meeting the sparkling eyes of Queen Elizabeth and attempting to return the smile of Prince Philip. As we shook hands we were well aware that our duty on this occasion was to bring the greetings of everyone in our constituency at home to the royal couple and through them to Canadians everywhere; and, yes, to the members of that great association of peoples throughout the world which our royal family represents.
It was very apparent here in Ottawa and in Hull as the crowds gathered from day to day, as the children cheered and the members of this parliament mixed happily together, that the royal couple have a unique power to bring us together on a common ground in joyous jubilation. For a time at least our newspapers, radio and television forgot the tragedies, crimes and fears which normally form their headlines, to unite across the country and bring us joyous news of every event which happened throughout the opening of this parliament by Her Majesty. Even if our royal family served no other purpose than to bring us happily together they should be cherished as irreplaceable. May it ever be thus.
We notice in the speech from the throne that it is the intention of the government to continue the Colombo plan, for which I am sure they are to be complimented. As was mentioned on the floor of this house this morning and at other times, it appears that we intend to use wheat as part of our contribution in that area. May I note that this will have a twofold message of good will,

The Address-Mr. S. H. S. Thompson first to the recipients in that area of southern Asia and other distant lands and, second, to the western wheat farmers. All too often in the past the only gifts which we as a nation seemed to think of were those of arms and weapons of war. These in some instances can have a twofold purpose, in that they may be used either for or against our best interests.
We note that there will be held shortly a dominion-provincial conference. While the government are conducting this conference I would ask them to keep in mind that the taxes paid by the people of Alberta are to a large extent collected by the dominion government in other provinces, and I charge them therefore with the job of ensuring that equalization payments are made in a fair and just manner.
It is with great pleasure that I note there is to be an increase in the old age security pensions. I may say that I had the privilege of campaigning strongly as a Social Crediter on this matter right from the beginning of the campaign, and that I was immediately joined by my C.C.F. opponent. My Conservative friend-and that can be taken literally, as we were school friends together-proudly announced at the first of these all-candidate meetings that he had no platform whatever, and proceeded to criticize me for the fact that I had one, but very shortly on this question at least he was very pleased to join ranks with us. In view of the fact that the Liberal party therefore appears to be the only party in opposition, there should be no trouble in bringing this legislation quickly to fruition.
In this connection, while of course this increase will bring assistance to many of our senior citizens throughout the land, I would like to mention another phase of the matter which was particularly brought home to me by the eventide home operated by the Salvation Army in our particular community. I might mention that a former member of the legislature of the province of Alberta is now living out his days there among old friends.
The people who pledge their lives to the work they are doing in providing homes and friendship for our senior citizens should not have to be perpetually plagued by financial problems as they have been in the past. Therefore the increase in pensions will carry a message of goodwill throughout all these organizations across the land.
However, I would ask one question about the next part of the speech from the throne. Is it wise to shorten the period of residence for qualification for the old age security pension? What effect will this have on the


amount of increase which will be available for those who are already entitled? Perhaps this shortening of the period is based on the assumption that those who pay into a fund should reap a benefit from it. If this is the case then may I ask the government to bear in mind the fact that a person may live in this country for the full 70 years of his productive life, yet when he receives his pension he may lose it again if his doctor suggests that for health reasons he should live in Arizona. Therefore I charge the government that if it is to consider the period of residence necessary to qualify, then it must also consider the period of residence necessary to disqualify.
We welcomed the announcement that blind allowances will be increased in proportion to the others. If any of you have not had the privilege of being associated with the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and meeting their executives, who in most instances conduct the business of that organization in total blindness themselves and do such a wonderful job of it, who come out into the seeing world among us and put forth the problems of their fellow men who are similarly afflicted, I say you have missed an education. You have been deprived of an important lesson in life if you have not had the privilege of attending some function held by the blind, usually very casual, at which they rise so easily, again in total darkness, to take part in whatever activity it may be.
As a veteran I welcome the increase in veterans allowances and pensions, and charge the Minister of National Defence to fight within the government a final and lasting battle to ensure that all veterans will secure a just allowance at this time. In conjunction with this I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West on his appointment to the position of parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence. I might say I have had the pleasure of being associated in business with the hon. member for Edmonton West, and look forward to him playing a vital role in securing those allowances which are so greatly required by veterans throughout the country.
The constituency which I represent contains a wide belt of excellent, black loam farm land extending around the southern and eastern edges of the city of Edmonton. This is, of course, a highly developed area in which there are many of the finest dairymen, poultry men, pig men and other producers, and the rich market gardens supplying the city of Edmonton. Many of these producers are known across the country for their efficiency.

What does the wheat question mean to us? As you know, the Minister of Agriculture has told those who grow wheat and rely on it to diversify production. If you are familiar with what happened in the case of eggs last year you will realize that in large part this has already been done. For a period of some six months eggs remained at the floor price. Comparisons are sometimes odious, but if you would compare the price which our farmers received during the six months including the middle of winter with the price received in the 'thirties you would find they were receiving less. This appears a strange situation, but we must commend the farmers for the job they have done in finding ways and means of producing efficiently in winter, which they could not do a short time ago. I would point out that while cash advances are most welcome they represent only a temporary measure, and this government must do its best in accepting the responsibility which rests with it through the Canadian wheat board, that of selling our wheat.
To a large extent the sale of wheat is more an internal problem than people realize. Each time we attempt to sell wheat the purchaser feels he should sell us something in exchange. This is called trade. We have protections for industry which are known as customs tariffs, taxes, duties, etc. In many cases we are therefore unable to import from the countries to which we can sell our wheat. When the Prime Minister said an attempt would be made to divert 15 per cent of our present purchases from the United States to countries that could use our wheat I think his statement was justified, and this represents practically the only method by which we can sell Canadian wheat without disrupting our own economy. I am not suggesting for an instant that duties are not needed for the protection of our industry. However, as a new member arriving here and visiting the office of stationery supplies I was surprised to note that the ink well, stapler and pair of scissors for which I signed-and which they said would be available for only one session and therefore must be carefully accounted for-were all made in the United States.
While the South Saskatchewan river dam project is important and worth while on its merits, I submit the time may not be ripe for proceeding with it if in doing so it is the intention to irrigate a large part of southern Saskatchewan and place there men to compete with those who work in the irrigated areas of Lethbridge and the highly developed special producing areas of Manitoba.
In the area from which I come we are faced with powerful competition from the
The Address-Mr. S. H. S. Thompson Lethbridge area, which is better developed and organized than our own. We are also confronted with keen competition from the distant area of southern California with regard to our vegetable products. I would therefore charge the government, when considering the South Saskatchewan river dam, with ensuring that there will be markets available for those who will farm that land and that we shall not add to our problems by launching a huge project prematurely, thus bringing about a situation in farming which is worse than the prevailing one.
The price spread between producers and consumers has been mentioned in this house. It is suggested that by investigating this circumstance we shall improve the situation. Usually when any investigation is going on those who are being investigated are in danger of being blamed. I am quite sure that the entire food industry will prove its strength and efficiency during this investigation. I might mention that during hurricane "Hazel" I had the privilege of being in Toronto to attend the convention of the retail merchants' association of Canada. At that time we were asked by the milk foundation whether we as retailers would give assistance in moving our butter surplus. In reply we suggested that this could be done simply by enclosing a coupon with family allowance and pensions cheques across the nation, and that by doing so it would promote the sale of butter, not only at that particular time but for a considerably longer period, for butter would be going to the homes of many people who were not accustomed to using it.
We received from the Minister of Agriculture what I thought was rather a strange reply, which in general suggested there was not a surplus of butter. However, it was not long until we found that a large quantity of butter had been sold to Poland at a price nearly equivalent to the price of margarine which we, the people of Canada, were eating and which we were importing almost entirely from the United States, at least the product from which margarine is made. I can assure hon. members that the food industry generally will be very pleased to extend invitations to them to visit their plants and their stores, as we have done in Edmonton, to find out just how this giant industry works.
In the bureau of statistics somewhere here in Ottawa-I have not found it yet-there are many facts concerning the food industry. In these facts you will find it is pointed out that generally speaking the entire industry works on lower margins, in comparison with sales, than practically any other industry. I would suggest that a fact-finding body composed of members of this parliament should
25$

The Address-Mr. S. H. S. Thompson do the job. It would be more appropriate to give this job to members of parliament than to pass it over to a royal commission.
There is another reason for the rising cost of food, and it is a very important one to consider. Some time ago our homes were equipped with a washboard and a clothes line at a total cost of perhaps $2.50. I am sure most of the homes of hon. members here today contain a dryer and an automatic washer worth perhaps $600 or $700. When compared with the price of the washboard and the clothes line the increase in cost is fantastic.
Many improvements have been made in the food industry, and most of them have been asked for by the housewife. There are ready mixes and prepared food, which relieve drudgery in the kitchen. There are items such as washed potatoes. I do not think in the fine modern home the housewife would appreciate our old custom of buying a 100-pound sack of potatoes and getting with it a large quantity of the good earth. I therefore charge the honourable lady member of the government to work toward the emancipation of the home-maker and impress upon the government the fact that it is quite all right for the home-maker to demand that which she wants, namely prepared foods. I might say that is the difference between our way of life and that of the totalitarian states, where somebody decides what everyone should have.
In our constituency we are very proud to have the University of Alberta appropriately situated on very nice grounds on the banks of the North Saskatchewan river. It has now, of course, been enhanced by the glorious Jubilee auditorium built so recently. In this connection I might say that Calgary also has one. In this regard we are, of course, interested in the grants being made by the Canada Council. We say they should be equitably distributed, and we trust the government will see that this is done. In so far as grants for culture across the country are concerned, it is our desire that these grants should not attempt to control culture. We are very proud of the varied cultures which are our heritage in the west. Our people have come from all around the world and have brought those cultures to us, and we trust it will be the policy of this government to encourage those various cultures rather than attempt to put them all in the same mould.
The international airport in Edmonton is now under construction in my constituency. The Minister of Transport was very pleased to take his place at the opening function at that airport. You can imagine his surprise when, instead of being handed a silver spade, he was handed a giant bulldozer. However, he


carried on very well and after a while was in charge of the controls in the midst of the proud assembly there. After his departure his wife climbed aboard and added an interesting part to our ceremony that day. I say to the Minister of Transport that he has accepted this airport as his baby, and we trust he will ensure that everything goes forward at full speed and that the problems surrounding it will receive his full attention.
I may say that already the municipality of Leduc in which the airport lies is rather concerned regarding some problems that are developing. As hon. members know, when you start to build an airport you move heavy equipment. There will be a continuous stream of trucks hauling gravel to this airport. We trust this government will assure the municipality of Leduc that it will repair or rebuild the roads which these gravel trucks may destroy.
Edmonton-Strathcona is one of the most progressive and fast-changing constituencies in Canada. At the end of the war there was only one factory of any size in the constituency, and that was the factory of Gainer's Limited. This was true until a few years ago. We now have the refineries of Imperial Oil, McColl-Frontenac, British American and the giant Celanese Corporation plant, which is a city in itself. The C.I.L. company have completed their plant and are developing their facilities very rapidly. I cannot claim the Sherritt-Gordon plant; it is just on the other side of the line, but most of its workmen live in the fast-growing town of Fort Saskatchewan, from which you will be hearing much in the future.
These industries have in turn brought subsidiary industries which either supply them or process their products. Many changes have taken place in our community. As all these industries work round the clock; there is continuous shift work and shift changing. We have now become accustomed to having our highways suddenly clogged as shift changes take place, and to having perpetual traffic throughout the night.
We are starting to realize more of the problems throughout the country and to feel a closer affiliation with the industrial east. We are also interested now in markets throughout the world, not only for wheat but for many other products as well. As you know, the production of the celanese plant will be seeking markets wherever they can be found anywhere in the world. Yes, the single wheat economy is leaving our area.
I come now to changes in taxation. I, of course, do not know at the moment what these may be, but I should like to mention

those which I feel are most important to my constituents. First of all there is the matter of the personal exemptions now provided under the Income Tax Act. The income tax of the average person in the country has been increasing continually as his wages have increased to keep up with the cost of living. This did not require any act of parliament. However, in order that he may be relieved of continually increasing income tax the exemptions must be increased. Over any considerable period, if wages continue to rise this would not necessarily mean any reduction in the return to the government from the income tax field.
May I also say a word about corporation income taxes. If it is the intention of the government to do anything in this connection I suggest that a similar policy should be adopted. In other words, the amount on which the 20 per cent levy is made, that is $20,000, should be increased in order to give small business a better opportunity, rather than to decrease the higher taxes on larger corporation profits. If it is the intention of the government to reduce the sales tax on cars I suggest that they keep in mind the position of the dealers holding cars and ensure that they are treated equitably.
In our urban area we of course have problems similar to those throughout the country, but in the fast moving city of Edmonton I think the housing shortage is more pronounced than in other places. At a time when immigrants were flooding into the city and we were reaching the period when the large increase in the birth rate of the war years was going to be felt in the number of young families seeking homes, action was taken to curtail house construction.
In addition, we saw the development of high interest rates, which meant that those providing the money suddenly had an increase in profits greater than the builders could ever hope to make in, the construction of houses.
I submit it is most important that our house-building industry be revived, for individual homes are the stronghold of democracy. We saw small business crushed and destroyed by the sudden imposition of a blanket policy across the country to protect us from supposed inflation. Financially strong companies could weather such a change but many solid, efficient firms were suddenly destroyed because they were caught short at that particular time. This was called a tight money policy and introduced to curb inflation.
Our Liberal friends have accused this party of having a policy which would create 96698-17
The Address-Mr. Van Horne inflation. It was certainly most interesting during the election campaign to be able to challenge them on what they meant by inflation. Mr. Speaker, rapid deflation could have a worse effect on the country than any inflation. I do not mean to say that rapid inflation is a good thing either, but rapid deflation represents in a way a strike of the top bracket organizers of industry and business across the land, of the men who have the know-how to develop Canada. This is no time for a pessimistic attitude, for I predict that regardless of what we may do Canada will surge on to claim the last part of this century as Canada's own.
Finally may I say that while I am sure it is the feeling of my constituents that in the house I should always criticize anything which affects their interests adversely, I am also sure it is their feeling that they elected me to come here and do a job. Therefore I shall always be ready to cooperate with the government as far as possible in attempting to ensure that this parliament shall continue in session and shall not become such a fiasco of procedural debate as that one which had for its excuse the trans-Canada pipe-line issue. I hope we will not hear anything more about closure, for it would appear that the government in power are the only ones who can use closure and if they were to eliminate it, it would suggest that they intend to be sitting in the opposition very shortly.

speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend to you my sincere congratulations upon your so well deserved appointment. I should like also, through you, to congratulate the Speaker of the house on his elevation to his very high office. As Her Majesty the Queen and Prince Philip return to England I know they leave in the hearts of all Canadians feelings of loyalty, gratitude and joy at the knowledge that we have a real Queen of Canada. I am sure she takes with her the best wishes of the Canadian nation.
I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Smith) and seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of
258	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Van Horne the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Certainly it is fitting that the address should be moved by a western member. When the hon. member for Bonaventure speaks of the backward conditions along the Gaspe coast, I can assure you that he speaks the truth. The Gaspe coast, like the maritime provinces, has been a neglected part of Canada for the past 22 years.
I wish to say a word to express to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) my sincere best wishes for many happy years in retirement. While we were celebrating the victory of June 10 in premises that had been arranged for long before the election, because we knew we were going to win, I could not escape noting that a great chieftain had fallen. Later I was pleased to hear that he intended to lead his party through the next general election. Then those young Liberals came from Ontario and decided to see how far they could go, aided and abetted by some of the Leader of the Opposition's own colleagues on his left and right, in criticizing their chief. This action strikes me as the height of ingratitude to a man who has given so much to his party and his country. Certainly I for one and many members of my party were quite willing to give the former government advice which, if followed, probably would have meant their re-election last June. However that may be it is well to reflect that my people, and the people of Canada, will long remember how these young, two-bit political hoodlums treated their chief after this last election. Our people can hardly wait for a chance to rid this country of the remnants of the soon to be leaderless Liberal party.
Quite apart from all this, sir, I wish to assure you that there has never been on my part, and there never will be, any feeling of animosity toward any member of this house, let alone the former prime minister. We come here to do a duty, sent here by the people we are elected to represent. My loyalty in the past has always been, and will continue to be, to the people I am here to represent, regardless of party politics. At the outset I should like to congratulate one minister of the new government who has done more for my riding, and for the maritime provinces, than any other minister of public works in the long history of Canada. I recall coming to Ottawa a few weeks ago on a Sunday night with Mr. Leo Hachey, the unsuccessful candidate in Gloucester county. This was just before the announcement had been made that $3.5 million had been made available to develop the harbour at Bathurst. I noted then that Mr. Hachey was doing more for his


riding, although he had not been elected, than all the Liberal members had been able to do during the past 22 years.
By the way, I should like to thank the exminister of national health and welfare for the help he gave me during the campaign. He was down in my area, and I am assured that if I received the largest majority in the history of Campbellton it was due in no small part to his efforts on my behalf.
For many years the port of Dalhousie had been a sore spot because the minister of transport had refused, times without number, to have it declared a year-round port, although it had been open for five consecutive years without expense to anyone. The only trouble that developed was ice forming in the gulf during two weeks one winter. No sooner had the election taken place than the present Minister of Public Works dispatched to my riding his chief economic adviser and other distinguished members of his staff. Even the editorials in the Liberal papers in my riding mentioned the fact that these officials came to us for the first time since confederation. We have been getting recognition for our problems that we have never been able to get before. It is indeed satisfying to learn that just last week arrangements were made, in collaboration with the president of the Canadian International Paper Company, whereby the port of Dalhousie will become a year-round port, and whereby a fine new wharf will be established there in the course of the next year.
The former government never quite appreciated our problems, because I am sure if they had they would have acted. This was due in part, I think, to the fact that Liberal representatives were so sure they would not be listened to that they did not see fit to speak. I can tell the former government that if it had taken, for instance, some of the advice given to it by the hon. member for Westmorland the result of the vote in the last election might have been quite different, especially in the maritime provinces. In any event the port of Dalhousie will now become a reality.
I should like to deal for a few moments with the Campbellton-Cross Point bridge. Twelve surveys have been made in connection with this bridge by various governments since confederation. Sets of plans have been drawn up and at various times estimates have been prepared. At election time these plans were hauled out and shown to the people. This bridge became a political football during one election after another. Now, less than 22 weeks after June 10 a proposal has been made whereby the federal government will undertake to pay $1,400,000 toward the cost

of that bridge, plus one-third of the balance. The government was paying $70,000 a year in subsidies and repairs to the ferry wharves. The government made a brief mathematical calculation and saw that the $70,000 a year would be better spent in taking care of a capital expenditure of something like $1,400,000.
Instead of expecting the two provinces and the dominion to each pay one-third of the cost, as the previous government had so often declared was its policy, the new government proposed to pay $1,400,000 plus one-third of the balance, leaving Quebec and New Brunswick each to pay one-third. When Hon. Hugh John Flemming received this proposal I was immediately summoned to Fredericton. Within five minutes of the commencement of our meeting to discuss this proposal it was accepted by the province of New Brunswick. The federal government has now been advised that New Brunswick accepts the proposal and is prepared to pay this one-third of the cost. We are waiting momentarily for word, which we understand will be forthcoming today or tomorrow, from the government of Quebec, indicating their approval in contributing in a like manner.
There is a concrete example of good business administration and a sound investment. There is an example of a government that is trying to do something for a part of the country which we all know was neglected for too long by too many governments.
I should also like to say a word of thanks in connection with the new federal building which will be going up in Campbellton. I should like to say a word of praise for the splendid co-operation we have been getting from the Minister of Transport, from the Prime Minister's office and from all branches of the government. Our people in the maritime provinces now know that we have in Ottawa a government that is prepared to sit down and listen to their problems and endeavour by all possible means to bring about a solution to those problems which have been ignored ever since confederation.
In connection with the throne speech I should like very much to express my gratitude. I know I speak on behalf of the people I represent when I say that this throne speech is indeed indicative of the new deal which this government is prepared to give to the people of the maritime provinces. How often in the past have we pleaded, in this house for help for Beechwood, and how often have those requests been turned down. Yet, I dare say there was not a man in this house who did not recognize the merits of that case and who did not in his own heart feel that something should be done. It was 96698-17*
The Address-Mr. Van Horne only because of the indifference of the past government that nothing had been done. Yet within weeks of taking office this new government has indicated in no uncertain way that the Beechwood project, along with the other four accompanying projects which will completely harness the Saint John river, costing as they will something like $215 million, will not be retarded because of lack of co-operation and help from this government.
Likewise as to electric power development in the entire maritime provinces; we are grateful that at last we have a government that is willing to help us out. We do not ask for favours. We are asking merely that we be given a chance to develop in the same manner as the rest of Canada has had a chance to do. We are indeed gratified, and the news in the throne speech fills the heart of every person in the maritime provinces with pride in the new government that is finally prepared to recognize its duty to do it.
I should like also to say a word in connection with social security. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that this government, which I am privileged to support, will take advantage of the opportunity it has to do everything possible to rid this country of the means test. I confidently expect that old age pensions will be increased to $60 a month and be made available to all Canadians at the age of 65.
I have been asked before where I stood in this house. As long as I am here I will continue to repeat the demands I have been making in the past. What I ask is reasonable. Certainly if the late government had implemented only a portion of those demands it would still be in office today. This is a case of not punishing people because they want to supplement their meagre pension by earning a few extra dollars while working some place in the summer months. It is a case of not punishing a person because he has had the courage to save a few dollars and has a little bank account of $1,000 or $2,000. It is a case of not punishing the father of a family who had the courage to save his money, and who is now denied that pension precisely because he had the courage. In my opinion the situation is most unjust, and this government will be unworthy unless it does everything within its power to bring about the abolition of the means test at the earliest possible moment.
I should like to say a word about the Chignecto canal. I realize that the canal has been another political football ever since confederation, at which time it was promised as part of the inducement offered to the maritime provinces to have them join confederation. As a supporter of this government I know it will not delay in appointing

The Address-Mr. Van Horne the commission which has been promised and which will be appointed to investigate all phases of this important canal. The Chignecto canal must be built. This government must recognize the fact that the canal was a premise upon which the maritime provinces entered confederation. I am sure this government will do that.
I should probably take a minute to speak of unemployment since it was mentioned by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) the other day. I realize that unemployment is a problem that has plagued the maritime provinces for years without number. In June there were 1,109 people unemployed in Camp-bellton. It is true that today there are something like 710 persons unemployed. This means that there are 339 or approximately one-third fewer unemployed than there were at the time of the election.
I certainly have investigated this problem. I have gone to the heads of all the pulp mills in my area. Their explanation is clearcut. They say that had it not been for the tight money policies of the late government, and were it not for the unfavourable exchange on United States money, our mills would be going at full capacity and all our people would be working.
I remember discussing this problem with the presidents and other officers of the Irving Pulp and Paper Company, and they decided- not entirely, I may say very frankly, without grave consideration and expense-to employ this year twice as many men as they employed last year in order to offset the unemployment situation that developed in that part of the province with regard to the lumber industry. In other words, instead of 1,000 men being in the woods cutting pulpwood for the Irving Pulp and Paper Company, there will be this year over 2,000 men.
I visited these camps some time ago and asked one man how much he was making cutting pulpwood. He said, "In the past three months I have averaged $24 a day". The International Paper Company told me that those employed by it doing similar work average $15 a day. Certainly those wages compare favourably even with the salary paid to a member of parliament, I might say. The management of the International Paper Company have also tried to do everything possible to put men to work early in the summer in order to offset unemployment.
So while possibly the hon. member for Charlotte and I are in agreement as to the grave dangers of unemployment, I may assure him, as I assure this house, that the industries operating in that area are not lacking

in knowledge of the situation and are not lacking in the desire to do everything possible to assist the workingmen of my riding.
What I was complaining about last year I shall be complaining about this year if the situation arises. I refer to delays in settling unemployment insurance claims. Those notices to which the hon. member for Charlotte referred were invitations to those people in my riding who were experiencing six weeks, seven weeks and eight weeks of delay in getting their unemployment insurance cheques to let me know about those matters. If this year these complaints can be handled by three stenographers that will be a help, because last year it would have taken twelve.
I should like also to speak briefly this afternoon with regard to housing. I am very grateful that this government has recognized the difficulties of the average wage earner in purchasing a home, and the $150 million which has now been made available by this government will certainly go a long way in providing houses for thousands of our families. But I say this in all frankness, as I have said it before in this house; that this is not sufficient. I have long advocated in this house, and I advocate again, the adoption of the American national housing act, lock stock and barrel. Why is it, if in the United States legislation can be introduced and properly carried out whereby a person can purchase a house with 4 per cent down of the first $10,000 and with nothing down in the case of a veteran, this government cannot do the same? I certainly see no reason why similar action would not be possible here in Canada.
There is nothing that gives more pride or satisfaction to a young father of a family as the knowledge that he can possess his own home. There is nothing which encourages good citizenship like property ownership, and nothing which would more effectively relieve the unemployment situation or would move our unsold lumber, of which our people down home have over 10 million feet in one yard alone, than an entirely new approach to our housing problem.
In the United States even the utensils in the kitchen, such as the electric stove, electric refrigerator, dryer, washer and even the fan that takes the smoke from the kitchen, are all included in the cost of the house. So a person who makes his down payment of $400 on a $10,000 home buys a house that comes to him almost fully equipped in regard to the heavy equipment which is needed in a modern home. If this system would cost this government anything I might take a different approach, but this government is making $15 million one year and $16 million

the next in profit under its national housing scheme. In the United States the same situation exists.
Why was the late government so afraid of the Canadian citizen that it would not trust him? There is not a valid reason that could be advanced as to why the down payments on homes could not be on the same scale as they are in the United States. There funds are provided with interest at 5J per cent, and there is no reason why funds could not be made available to the Canadian people in like manner. There is also no reason why we in Canada, under our housing scheme, could not recognize the loan value of a house already built. The effect of our housing scheme is to diminish the equity which people have in homes already built outside of our national housing scheme.
It seems unfortunate that the late government did not recognize its duties in this connection. Goodness knows, and I have spoken about this often in the house, if we are to solve our housing problem we have to do what has been done successfully in other countries. I remember in one little operation, in a town where a housing project was started, 104 people applied for homes. Yet not one person was able to purchase a home because not one person had the $3,000 or $4,000 needed for a down payment. Certainly I trust that this government will take every occasion to make sure that the National Housing Act, as we know it, is altered to meet the needs of the Canadian people.
I would like to say something about agriculture. In my riding since June 10 something like $400,000 has been expended in an effort to help the potato farmers in the northern part of New Brunswick. This help is certainly very much appreciated, but four or five weeks ago our small potato farmers had upwards of 600,000 barrels of potatoes which they were unable to sell and which they were unable to keep because of the lack of proper storage facilities. If a diversion program had been undertaken at that time I feel sure that the small potato farmer would have been greatly helped; and I know that although everything possible has been done since June 10, a whole new approach to agriculture as it exists in northern New Brunswick should be undertaken.
I should like also to say a word of commentary in regard to a statement made last Friday by the member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier). If ever there was a party in this country which pitted religion against religion, race against race and province against province in a deceitful effort to gain votes during the past 20 years, it was the Liberal party. I come from a riding where the population
The Address-Mr. Van Horne is 85 per cent French speaking or Acadian, and I know whereof I speak. In the past I have no doubt that under the vigorous leadership which existed in the Liberal party those tactics were not permitted to be mentioned in this house. Now, however, when the Liberals are about to become leaderless, they have brought these tactics into the open in the House of Commons. I could tell you stories of happenings in my own riding that would make your hair stand on end with respect to disgraceful tactics in bringing race and religion into elections. It is a disgrace to the member who brought up the subject in this house. It was bad enough when they kept it behind closed doors, as in the past.
Before taking my seat I would like to mention one more subject. I presume this combines investigation into pulpwood fixing prices may have had its place, but I wish to state publicly here that I very much disapprove of the actions taken by members of that investigation committee or board in their conduct with many of the officials of our paper companies. I know of one instance where after rifling through the files in the president's office, they took advantage of his absence to go and rifle his desk without any form of authority from any court.
We are determined, and I know this government will take every opportunity to do this, to rid these services of the Gestapo methods which have been customary in the past. The people who operate these industries, the people who operate these mills, have a hard enough time getting along without the government interfering as it has done. I maintain that this investigation was properly set up, but it miscarried and was conducted in such a way as to bring discredit on the Department of Justice and the government as a whole. Certainly we have a right to expect a different kind of attitude, and I know we will have a different kind of attitude from now on.
Before resuming my place I invite hon. members on both sides of the house to give us a hand in the maritime provinces. I know we will have to await another election before we will have 10 Conservative members from New Brunswick, but in the meantime we urge the five Liberal members to not stint their efforts to co-operate with us to bring about the improvements we have so long needed in the province of New Brunswick and indeed in the maritime provinces generally.
In closing I would like to say I am very grateful and glad to be seated on this side of the house, but I wish to make it very clear at the same time that our problems are above party politics, and the needs of our people

The Address-Mr. Gardiner demand immediate action. While it is a pleasure to work and co-operate within the framework of a party may I assure you, as I assure this house, that the duty I owe to the people of my riding and to the people of the maritime provinces will always come first.

Mr. Speaker, in the first place I should like to join with those who have spoken before me in congratulating the hon. member who was chosen as Speaker of the house on the first day we met, and to say to him I feel confident that in the period he occupies the chair of this house he will do so-and we are acknowledging that he does so-by maintaining the traditions of the speakership. During the long history of Canadian parliaments I think there has been no occasion upon which the Speaker himself was responsible for any unnecessary scenes which may have taken place in this house.
I would also like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Arsenault), is not very well known to me and I regret that I am not sufficiently familiar with the language which is his natural language to have followed him closely throughout the entire course of his remarks, but I am assured from the discussions which have taken place since that he fulfilled his duty in a manner which is most acceptable to the house.
As far as the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne is concerned, I have been familiar with his family for a long time. His dad and I knew one another well in our school days when we took part in college and other sports. He was always known as Sport Smith, which indicated that he was not only a good athlete but that he had the proper attitude toward the game he was playing and toward both those who were with him and against him.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
