speechtext:
As we listened to our young friend, his son, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) as he made his first speech in the house the other day I was reminded of the fact that in those days his grandfather used to walk up and down the field where a game was being played and every time one of the boys kicked, he kicked too and gave the best of encouragement to those of his family who were participating in the game.
I am sure had he been present the other day sitting in the gallery-and if he had been following the same line of thought he followed in those days he would have been


sitting in the gallery facing the opposition, but it would not have made any difference where he was sitting-and, had been listening to our young friend deliver his first speech in this house, he would have been extremely proud of his grandson. So would his dad had he been able to be here. I am not sure whether his uncle who lives in Regina was here the other day, but he too would have been proud of our young friend and would have followed his remarks with keen interest. I understand his mother was present, and I am sure she felt proud of the capable manner in which her son made his maiden speech.
These people were all friends of mine and friends of Saskatchewan in the early days. They lived in Regina and conducted an important business there in the pioneering days. We all acknowledge them for what they have done for us and share their pride in this young member of their family to whom was given the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I personally wish him every success.
I should now like to refer to what has been mentioned by most speakers who have participated in this debate, namely the 10-day period immediately past during which Her Most Gracious Majesty was present on this continent, four days of which were spent in association with the opening of parliament and other matters in this capital city of Canada and the other six in connection with the affairs of the country to the south. I think this 10-day period will go down in history as one Which has done more to promote the best interests of the commonwealth of nations, and through the commonwealth the best interests of all the people in the world, than any other 10-day period in the entire history of the commonwealth.
To watch the proceedings of yesterday on television when the Queen was in the city of New York, and to have observed the previous proceedings when she was in the city of Washington, would suggest to one that at least those people on the other side of the line who associate their beginnings with Great Britain, and perhaps not less the people whose ancestors came to this continent from other parts of Europe, where they had monarchies for a long period of time, were very proud of the fact that the race to which many of them belong could produce a sovereign of the type we have today as Queen of Canada and Queen of the other nations of the commonwealth.
Just an hour ago I heard over the radio that the royal plane had arrived at the London airport. I am sure we all congratulate Her Majesty upon her fine appearance on this

continent and upon the fact that she and her husband have arrived back home safely.
Before going on to say more I think I should ask why we are here and try to give an answer as to why, in my opinion, we are gathered in this parliament. I am not speaking so much about the fact that for the first time I am sitting in the opposition in the House of Commons, which is a rather new experience for me. I have spent 44 years in politics. Out of that period I have been in opposition for only five years, and during that period of five years I was leader of the opposition in the legislature of Saskatchewan. So I cannot complain about the treatment I have received from the voters of the province of Saskatchewan and more particularly of my own constituency over that long period of time. Finding ourselves on this side of the house we must of necessity ask not only why we are here but we must attempt to answer the question why we are taking the position we are with regard to certain matters.
In the first place I might point out that this house was dissolved in April before we had voted all our estimates. As a matter of fact we had voted only a small part of them. At that time full expressions of opinion had not been given about a considerable part of the legislation which had been introduced in the house by the government of that time. It is probably going too far to say that the new government is in any way responsible for the legislation which was introduced but not passed, and of course we do not expect that it will be reintroducing that legislation in the house in the form in which it was then brought down either now or at any other time. On the other hand the system under which we operate presupposes that the money required for the conduct of the affairs of this country must be voted by parliament. Dissolution of the house at the time it took place resulted in that money not being voted; therefore it is necessary for us to be here at this time in order to see that that vote is carried through.
Of course we do not expect, and it has not been the case, that the present government is going to agree in every particular with the legislative program and the votes that were brought down by the preceding government, but it will be necessary to vote in general the greater part of the funds which were to have been made available through the estimates at that time, and we are here for that purpose.
Since that time we have had an election which has produced certain results. Every member of this house knows that under our constitution the leader of the party which can command a majority in the House of
The Address-Mr. Gardiner Commons is called upon to form the government. Therefore on this occasion when the people of Canada did not select any party with a majority of seats in this house; at a time when they gave to the Liberal leader the greatest number of votes in his favour obtained by any person but gave to the leader of the Conservative party the greatest number of seats given to any party, then it stands to reason that we are in a very peculiar situation at the present time.
This is not new to me at all, because most hon. members know that I went through a similar experience in Saskatchewan back in 1929, although there was this difference then. Although we did not have a majority we had the largest group. I was advised then, and I am advised now, that under our constitution when the government itself has the largest group following an election but there is no majority in the house in their favour, it is necessary for them to meet the house. They should meet the house and have the house determine as to who should be responsible for forming the government.
On this occasion the government party did not have the largest group. I am advised that under the constitution, in those circumstances, it is not necessary but is a matter of choice with the leader of the party which forms the government for the time being as to whether he should meet the house or whether he should advise the Governor General to call upon some other member of the house to form the government. Well, the leader of the government decided on the latter course, that is was advisable to go to the Governor General and discuss with him the possibility of resigning and not meeting the house, and turning the government over to some other party.
Well, naturally on an occasion of that kind the first thing the Governor General would want to know, the first thing a representative of the crown would want to know, is how do you propose that the government should be able to carry on sufficiently long to make it possible for the people of this country to know as to whether the person to whom they have given the largest representation is a person who can command a majority? There was only one way in which that information could be given to the Governor General, and that was for his adviser of that day to give it. Before going to see the Governor General the leader of the government naturally went to see the leader of the official opposition, who had the largest group in the house, and found him not only willing but anxious to form a government and take the responsibility for setting up a government under our democratic institution.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
When the government of the day found it necessary to give assurance to the Governor General those assurances, of course, were given to the effect that we would carry on in such manner as to make it possible for the new government to have sufficient support in the house to be able to place their policies before the people of this country and carry on from there.
I recite these facts in order to say this, Mr. Speaker. I find it a little difficult to understand some of the criticisms that are made at the present time of the attitude of the present opposition. Before going on to speak further with regard to that point I would call attention to this also. Before the prime minister of that time went to the Governor General to discuss the matter the leaders of the two smaller groups in this house gave interviews to the press, in which they stated that they were not prepared to join in a coalition with either of the larger parties, but that they were prepared to give whichever party undertook to carry on sufficient support to allow it to make it apparent in what direction they wanted to go after forming a government or continuing as a government.

He says "too long". Since we had been in power a long time they thought we should turn over the government to some other group, and therefore they supported our turning the government over to the Conservatives. I am quite sure I am correct-I am sorry I did not bring the clippings from the papers with me-when I suggest that sufficient assurance was given to the party which now forms the government that if they did form the government they would be given an opportunity to make their views known to this house before they were voted out.
Therefore I say, with regard to the official opposition of today, that we feel we owe an obligation not only to the government of the day, not only to the group who form a minority in this house and who form the government, but we owe a duty to the crown and to the people of Canada to see to it that the affairs of this house are conducted in such a manner as to permit of the government placing their views on certain matters,


on legislation, on the budget and on estimates, squarely before this house with their support and their recommendations to the Governor General behind them.
Before there was any thought of choosing a new Liberal leader in this country the prime minister of the day made the announcement, when he tendered his resignation, that he had given those assurances to the Governor General; that we would carry them out, and at the time he gave the assurance that it was his declared intention to lead the Liberal party in the next election in this country. When it is suggested here by some critics that anything we do in this house has anything to do with the fact that a Liberal convention is to be held to elect a leader, I want to say to the house and to the people of this country that the whole matter under discussion was settled before it became necessary to choose a leader at all.
I do want to say this-I have not consulted with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) or anyone else about this-that so far as I am personally concerned and I think so far as most of the Liberal members, or all the Liberals in Canada are concerned, if the press which is advocating such a policy, or if those on the other side of the house think it is a good line to follow, there would be nothing that would be more helpful to the Liberal party in the next election, whenever it may be called, than that we should be fighting it under the leadership of the present leader of the Liberal party. I wanted to say that in order to leave the impression that it had nothing to do with the matter of our giving assurances under the constitution as it exists that we would give the government an opportunity to place their policies before the house and the people of the country before we would consider it necessary to move a vote of want of confidence.
I would like to submit, Mr. Speaker, that I think the smaller groups would have been well advised to follow at least the intimation that was made prior to the calling of the house and to have desisted from moving votes of want of confidence at this stage. While this party is not moving a vote of want of confidence, it does not mean that we have absolute confidence in the government.
It does indicate that our constitution has got to be allowed to operate. At the same time I feel personally, believing as I do that the two opposition groups had given an assurance very similar to the one we had given, that they are moving their motions of want of confidence at too early a stage in the development that has taken place since the election. So as far as I personally am

concerned I am going to vote against both of them. When I do vote against both of them I will not necessarily be voting against anything that may be in either one of them, but I will be voting against the fact that two considerable groups in the house, having given everyone to understand that they would allow the constitution to operate, are placing party above the welfare of the country at the present time.
We in this group do not intend to do that. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that we should get on with the business we came here to do, namely to provide the money with which the government is going to be able to carry on until March 31. That is really the only work we came here to do. When the government finds it necessary to make some changes, slight or otherwise, in the provision for the spending of that money we must, of course, give consideration to that, and express our opinions as we go along; but in my opinion we should get on with the business of providing supply, clearing the order paper of legislation necessary to authorize expenditures and return to our homes until the government is prepared to bring in legislation and a budget and estimates they are prepared to recommend to the Governor General which will set out a policy based upon their criticisms of the last government and their election promises.
I would judge from what has been said and the attitude taken by the leaders of the party facing us that is what they intend to do. Of course if they intend to do that they will expect that some members on this side of the house may raise some objection to some of the things they are suggesting should be done which the previous government had not intended to do had it remained in office, but I think they will find that if they can listen to the expression of opinions on those matters without too strong political feelings resulting from such expression we will get along fairly well to the end of this particular session.
There is only one further remark I should like to make with regard to this discussion, and it is this. I was a little surprised at the attitude taken by the Minister of Finance early in the discussion, when he rose in his place at a time when the Prime Minister was not here-there is no criticism in that; I think he was in Washington-and said in effect that he intends to make all members in the house stand up and be counted on every occasion when any advance is being made on any estimates.

Therefore I would suggest that if we can all accept the position that we are here to do the particular job that ought to be done, we can express our criticisms from any place in the house from time to time, put them on the record and refer to them in times to come when we desire to do so.
It is not my intention to spend any more time on that matter in dealing with the speech from the throne. It is my intention to spend most of my time on past and present proposals with regard to agriculture. But I must first call attention to the similarity between the campaign of 1930 and the one just past. Quite a number of those who have spoken since the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) spoke last Friday have chosen to use his remarks as the basis for a discussion of an old issue that has been present in this country for a long time. But I should like to remind hon. members that this is not a new and unheard of situation. Prior to 1930 and after Mr. Bennett had been chosen leader of the Liberal-the Conservative party; I think it was Liberal-Conservative at that time-his supporters decided to put on a sham battle in a section of Canada that had never been anything but Liberal since it came into confederation, and that sham battle was fought on the issue that has been referred to in the debate here.
It had the result of electing eight members of that party from the province of Saskatchewan, which is the most it has ever elected either before or since that time. The election which followed a year later was won by Mr. Bennett and his party and he came into office. It does not make any difference what members on the other side of the house think. It is quite proper that they should think whatever they wish about the matter, but it has some effect when I hear persons get up and object to criticisms being made when everyone in the house and the country knows that this has been an issue between two sections of Canada over a long period of time. The introduction of certain ideas into the Conservative party convention last year did introduce the

The Address-Mr. Gardiner subject whether or not anyone said anything about it. So we had a section of the country that for two elections had been more strongly Liberal than at any other time in our history reverse its position and go to the opposite extreme in its voting.
It is all very well for members of the house and people outside the house to try to convince themselves that some other issue decided the last election, that it had something to do with economics, something to do with other things. All I want to say to the government is that if they are of that opinion they have an even greater task before them in 1957 in satisfying the people that they can create a better economic situation than Mr. Bennett had before him in 1930. I think the more you think about that the more you will agree it is correct.
Mr. Bennett had other ideas that were similar to those that are held now. He thought it was necessary to call a session of the house right after the election in 1930, as a matter of fact in September also, and he called that session. I sat in the gallery some place-I had great difficulty in getting into the galleries at all-and listened to the speech he delivered to the house on that occasion. In that speech he reviewed a considerable number of the things he had said during the campaign, and he said, "We are here to put them into effect."
Well, there is no doubt that he did put them into effect. If there ever was a man who led a party in the Dominion of Canada, who advocated conservatism and put it into effect when he came into office, that man was Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, later Lord Bennett. He put those ideas into effect.
Now, what was the result? He had stated in that campaign-note the similarity of subject-put me in and I will pay 100 per cent of old age pensions. Did he ever do it? No, he did not. He did get it up to 75 per cent at one time, but he did not get it any further than that. I sat in a legislature at that time and they did not bring down a dollar to pay their 50 per cent share of the old age pension, with the result the legislature had to be called upon at a later date to vote the money because the federal government could not carry out its policy.
I listened a few moments ago to the hon. member speaking about Chignecto. I do not know if that is the way it should be pronounced but I think that is about right. Here is what Mr. Bennett said about that, according to the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of July 1, 1930:
We offer you the St. Lawrence waterways; the Chignecto canal is a possibility, yes, even a probability.


He said this in Saint John, right in the neighbourhood from which my friend who has just spoken comes. We have had two governments since those days and we have not got a Chignecto canal. We have had two governments since then and it was the second one, the Liberal government, which built the St. Lawrence waterway.
I hope our friends are not going to do as Mr. Bennett did in 1930, bring policies into this house in a rush in the first session a few weeks after an election. He pushed them through with his majority and made it absolutely impossible to pay 100 per cent of old age pensions. These policies made it absolutely impossible for him to build the St. Lawrence waterway or the Chignecto canal, and later made it impossible for him to carry on with the trans-Canada highway system, which had been introduced by Mr. Meighen, or the Trans-Canada Air Lines system, which had been introduced by Mr. King. The policies he introduced in that short session, without having given sufficient thought to them, raised great issues with the result that in 1935, speaking in New York. Mr. Bennett said this:
I say that tariffs in many ol the countries in the world today are much too high.
This is after he had been in office for five years. I could read earlier statements made to the effect that he was going to cure everything with tariffs.
He continued in New York:
I say that tariffs in Canada are too high.
One could go on reading statement after statement by Mr. Bennett indicating that after five years experience he had learned that it was not a good thing, either for the party or for the country, to rush legislation through the house without much consideration.
I believe I have said sufficient to indicate that there are similarities between the party of that day and the party of the present day. There is a little more to which I would like to call particular attention with regard to agricultural conditions. Mr. Bennett, speaking in Winnipeg on June 9, 1930, said this:
Listen, you agriculturists from the west and all the other parts of Canada, you have been taught to mock at tariffs and applaud free trade. Tell me, when did free trade fight for you? You say tariffs are only for the manufacturers. I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.
Anyone on the other side of the house, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) if he wished, could say that tariffs did work in the case of butter. They have. Governments since have continued what Mr. Bennett

did with regard to butter. However, I believe it will be found difficult to suggest that these policies worked in any other place in the interests of agriculture. One policy was the use of higher tariffs, together with quotas arranged at conferences. This is another similarity. A conference was held immediately after the election, and another one was held in 1932. Out of these conferences came policies which ruined the agriculture of this country. My friend shakes his head. I would suggest to him that he go over to the apple growing country of Great Britain, as I was invited to do two years ago. He will find there one family which, under the preference forced upon Great Britain by two dominions in 1932, has a third as many apple trees as there are in the whole of Nova Scotia and a quarter as many as there are in the whole of British Columbia. In other words, when you try to force your way into the markets of the world, and to control your marketing of products by the use of tariffs, you can do yourself much more harm than good.
During that period under these preferences these people have put in more new apple trees than we have in the whole of the Dominion of Canada. Since Britain has planted more new apple trees during that period than we have in Canada how could we expect to sell many apples in Great Britain? One has to give most careful consideration to these policies as we go along.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), speaking at Portage la Prairie during the last campaign stated, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of May 10, as follows:
The Liberal government is doing nothing while the United States attacks Canada's wheat markets with almost ruthless abandon.
He called for several measures to regain markets, including an approach to Britain to take wheat in place of some $17 million In interest owed to Canada on a postwar loan.
It is true that this statement does not mention tariffs, but some of the others do. Tariffs were mentioned as a means of taking care of this situation. Not very long ago the Minister of Agriculture announced that he was advancing the date on which fowl would be prevented from coming into this country. It would come into this country under the conditions set up by the order in council which we passed. I must say that at the time I discussed the matter with the officials of the department and the government, I was advised that fowl did not come into this country in any considerable numbers until August 1 and therefore we made it August 1. I would say it is a sort of bid for votes to tell the people of Canada under those circumstances you are advancing the date two weeks to the middle of July and say, "We 96698-18i
The Address-Mr. Gardiner are going to apply the same thing as the previous government, but two weeks in advance."
Then there was the announcement that there would be a duty on turkeys. The only reason there had not been something done about turkeys before was that turkeys were selling at 6 cents per pound higher in Canada than they were in the United States. That is the reason products come to this country from the United States or from anywhere else, the person who produces them and has them for sale can sell them at higher prices here than in their own country. If you want to stop that, there are two or three ways of doing it, but the Conservative way of doing it is to use tariffs. Another way would be to use embargoes. May I say to the government that they have been doing a lot of talking about ways and means of dealing with our wheat problem. The biggest obstruction to the proper disposal of our wheat in this world is right on this continent.
Prior to the last war there was a duty of 42 cents on our wheat going to the United States. When the president got the authority to reduce that he made it 21 cents, but just prior to that they imposed an embargo on our wheat so it could not go in at all.
Those are two ways of performing. If the government desires to perform in either one of them they will run into some difficulties which will give them considerable trouble over the weeks that are ahead. So I would again warn those who have been talking in the election of 1957, as their predecessors did in 1930, to study the aftermath of the action of their predecessors in the session of 1930 and to avoid the mistakes of that earlier time. This government should ask support at this session to do only what must be done now and should call us back to consider their well-thought-out policies early in the new year.
When the Liberals took over in 1935 we had two trans-Canada railway systems, a telegraph line and a telephone line to provide communication across Canada. When we turned the country back to the Conservatives in 1957 those railway systems were greatly developed, along with our telephone system and our telegraph system. But in addition to that we had a trans-Canada highway system which a world traveller said, as reported the other day in a newspaper, was one of the best that he found anywhere in the world.

The Address-Mr. Winch

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to every word just spoken by the former minister of agriculture. Having regard to the majority of the time he took and what he said, out of the generosity of my heart the best I can say is that never has it taken so long to say so little. To me the majority of his speech seemed to be only an expression of the rabid fears of the Liberals that they may be forced to face an early election. When added to the other speeches to which I have listened emanating from the Liberal side of the house, it can only be interpreted as an admission of the fact that in the general election campaign and since this house has met they have been caught with their political pants down and now they are trying desperately to cover up the fact that they are exposed.
I noticed that the hon. member who immediately preceded me went out of his way, and made it a point to do so, to go after the C.C.F. because we had moved an amendment to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. May we make it emphatically clear that we deliberately moved an amendment to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne and that we did so as a matter of fundamental principle and not as a matter of expediency.
We in the C.C.F. recognize the fact, as do most others, that although we welcome and will support

and have so stated-the beneficial proposals that have been mentioned in the speech from the throne, we differ in basic economic principle. We believe that the government, despite all it has said it is going to do, has missed the boat in connection with fundamental policies that will meet and solve the problems of this nation and will give and guarantee full employment, security and prosperity to the people of Canada. Because of the failure of the government to recognize that fact we have moved, as a fundamental principle, an amendment to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am most grateful to the voters of Vancouver East for the fact that they saw fit to return me as a result of the poll taken on June 10. I feel absolutely sure that this is going to be a most interesting and intriguing session. Those of us who have been here previously cannot help but be amused at the session thus far in seeing the Liberals, as an official opposition, screaming to high heaven because they cannot get answers to their questions or do the things they want to do, things which they denied when they were on the other side of the house; and then at the same time to

see the Conservatives, in what they have done thus far, giving exactly the same type of administration of parliamentary procedure as the Liberals gave previously and which they the Conservatives screamed to high heaven against. This sham battle would be most amusing if it were not actually so crucial. That is the way in which I want to introduce what we have to say.
Just as the previous Liberal government did not do so, the present Conservative government is not facing up to the real facts of Canadian life, the Canadian economy and developments throughout the world. Already this session we have heard from the parties of free enterprise-all three of them-a denouncement of the public ownership policies of the C.C.F. and a denouncement of the requisite social and economic planning as government policy which we say is so necessary at this time. Yet not only have we seen it year by year under the past government, but now we see through the medium of the speech from the throne the recognition by the present Conservative government that, in part at least, the future of Canada depends upon the co-operation of the federal authority and the provincial authorities in the realm of development under public ownership.
Knowing the free enterprise spirit of the other three parties, but in particular that of the Conservative government, may I say that this preliminary recognition must have been brought about because circumstances have forced it. We see it in the announcements already made of joint participation between the federal and provincial authorities in British Columbia on the Columbia river development, with the government of Saskatchewan on the Saskatchewan dam and, as mentioned by one hon. member-I think it was the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne)-on development in New Brunswick.
That is good, Mr. Speaker, as far as it goes but it is not going to solve the problem. Much as we welcome increases in pensions and allowances, that is not going to solve the problem either. Analysis will show that the only answer is an accelerated, deliberate policy of greater participation between the federal government and provincial governments on the development of natural resources under public ownership.
If that policy is not soon established then Canada is going to suffer from betrayal by, not only the past but the present government; because the way things are going today, in certain provinces under free enterprise governments there just are not going to be

any natural resources left as a heritage for the people of those provinces and the people of Canada generally.
Here we have, or we should have, recognition that Canada spent billions of dollars to fight and win a military war, not so many years ago at that. Now having won the military war we find our natural resources being handed away to those against whom we fought and those who lost the war. We are rapidly finding ourselves in the position where those who lost the war, under private enterprise policies in Canada are approaching the position where they own a great deal of our country.
Take the situation in British Columbia where there are now 71,000 square miles of that great province which have been handed over to the Wenner-Gren interests. One can pick up the paper every week and read of the infiltration of industry by the Krupp interests and others into the Canadian economy.
Now no one is going to oppose the development of our country, but if the major benefits of the wealth produced through the development of our natural resources is to remain in Canada then surely common sense dictates the policy to be established in the public interest is public ownership by cooperation between the governments of Canada. If the members of the free enterprise governments of the provinces are not prepared to go that far, if the free enterprise parties in this house are not prepared to go that far, and if the government now in office is not prepared to go that far, then surely it is not asking too much that they insitute policies to give the greatest possible return to the people of Canada to whom the heritage of our natural resources belongs and whose work produces the wealth.
It is with a great deal of regret that we in this corner of the house have to note that there is no indication whatsoever of this recognition, nor is there any indication of a line of action being taken and policies established which will retain in this country to the greatest possible extent the wealth produced here. We have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that it is wrong that outside capital can come into the country and reap untold millions of dollars' profit and yet pay no tax to the Canadian people through the medium of a capital gains tax.
Coming down from Vancouver to Ottawa I had a most interesting discussion with two very wealthy Americans on the train. They told me how much they loved Canada and I replied that I understood that because of our beautiful scenery, our natural resources and so on and so forth. They said we do not
The Address-Mr. Winch mean that, what we mean is that Canada is the land of golden opportunity for the profiteers. They told me quite honestly, knowing that I was an M.P. and a socialist one at that, that what they were doing was getting their capital out of the United States, putting it into Canada and leaving it here. I asked why, and they told me it was because there is no capital gains tax in Canada.
Time does not permit me, and I do not think it is even necessary because you, Mr. Speaker, should know from the records- especially with respect to the gas lines and oil pipe lines-that what has and is taking place is legal, financial highway robbery. This was pointed out by my leader who referred to the activities of the robber barons during the past months and years. If the government will not recognize the responsibility of public ownership in order to hold our natural resources for Canada, if they will not go along-and they have already said they will not-with a capital gains tax, then is it unreasonable to expect that the government and the government agencies should live up to the laws of Canada and that Canadians should not be made to subsidize Americans in the export of our raw materials to the United States.
Only a short time ago we had the opening of the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited operations in British Columbia. I made an investigation of what took place and I thought it was a matter for action by the Department of Justice but have since found that there is no legal action there, at least as far as it comes under that department. In the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited operation, under their present contract they are going to sell 500 million cubic feet of natural gas per day. Of that, 200 million cubic feet per day is contracted for by the B.C. Electric in British Columbia at a price of 32 cents a thousand and at a demand rate of 90 per cent.
Now they branch off to the United States at Huntington I believe, just alongside of
B.C. Electric's takeoff, but immediately that gas crosses the border, coming down the same pipe line, 200 million cubic feet per day is supplied to the United States company at 22 cents per thousand cubic feet. I would like to know why the citizens of British Columbia should have to pay almost 50 per cent more for our own gas on the whosesale basis than the cost to the wholesaler when it crosses the border into the United States.
I, through you, Mr. Speaker, most certainly direct these questions to the Conservative government in view of all their talk in this house during the past five years, in view of their campaigning across the country prior

The Address-Mr. Winch to June 10 about Canada first and the protection of Canadians, and how "we were not going to be rooked by the United States interests." Would they explain why the present situation has been allowed to develop. Not only, as I say, has the situation been allowed to develop, but this is something which I maintain is contrary to the law of Canada because we have an act entitled Exportation of Power and Fluids and the Importation of Gas Act. In the regulation of this act, which has not been repealed because I checked up on that, it says
The price charged by a licencee for power or gas exported by him shall not be lower than the price at which power or gas, respectively, is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.
That is a regulation in effect made under authority of an act of parliament. We want to know why a law enacted by this House of Commons is not lived up to. Even if there were no law, what is the political morality of a government that will allow a situation of this kind to continue?
I want to be absolutely honest. I believe this was the first such contract ever made in Canada and perhaps it slipped by those who are responsible for its ratification as far as the government or one of its agencies is concerned. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, may we ask assurance from the present government that there will be no repetition anywhere in Canada and that there will be a close scrutiny made of all contracts which may be presently under consideration or approaching consumation to ensure that the regulation will be lived up to and that Canadian consumers will not be placed in the position of subsidizing United States consumers in the export of our own raw materials.
I am certain the cabinet ministers from British Columbia will look into the point I am about to raise. I hope they will investigate the possibilities of examining into the re-drafting of the contract now in operation and which covers a period of 20 years. That is all I want to say on that matter at this time; but I wish to deal somewhat briefly with something else although it is a most important question.
A number of hon. members have spoken already on the question of unemployment and I feel I must, too, because of my knowledge of the situation as it exists in British Columbia and because on checking with the appropriate department I find, as I suspected was the case, that on a percentage basis unemployment in the Pacific region is higher than elsewhere in Canada.


During the past few months more than ever before I have been approached as a member of parliament by people in search of employment who were unable to find it. According to official figures I have been able to secure there were 29,138 registered unemployed in the Pacific region in September of this year as compared with 15,892 in the same week a year ago. In the city of Vancouver, one constituency of which I have the honour to represent, there were 15,141 registered unemployed on September 12 this year as compared with 8,019 in the same week a year ago. When you have an increase of almost 100 per cent in unemployment within a 12-month period it is a situation that cannot and must not be ignored.
I regret the evasiveness of the answer I received from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) the other day when I asked what action was contemplated by his department in meeting the unemployment problem. Whether there are 100 or 100,000 unemployed we have to be interested because these people are hungry. A great many of them are not covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act and with regard to those who do come under the act there is the essential need for an increase in the allowance paid comparable at least to the increases contemplated under other acts.
I wonder how many members of this house, especially those who are married, could pay rent and live on the amount paid under the act today with the existing high cost of living? It cannot be done. The allowance paid under the act is too little to live on and too much to die on; it should be better than that. We certainly hope that the matter is under active consideration and that immediate action will be taken. We hope also the government will not wait for some future dominion- provincial conference to determine federal financial responsibility before extending benefits to those who are not covered by the act.
Time after time such people have come to my home; they have no unemployment insurance either because they are not eligible for it or because it has run out. They are being evicted from their homes for non-payment of rent and find themselves with nothing to eat and no means of providing for their family. Where do we send them? In most instances the best we could do is send them down to the community council where they can get assistance for one, two, or perhaps three days; but what do they do then? M.P.'s cannot support them.
I cannot stress too strongly the seriousness of this situation. I believe that if the federal government would not wait for the . proposed

conference but would immediately notify the departments of labour of all the provinces that it is prepared to pay 50 or 60 per cent of the assistance to those not covered by the act prompt action would be taken in most provinces. I constantly encounter unemployed individuals in Vancouver who come to me for advice and assistance. I sincerely hope something will be done immediately and that it will be based on a decent standard.
In the few minutes left at my disposal I wish to draw to the attention of the government one other matter. I ask the government not to plan just from day to day but to look forward with creative vision. Despite all the questions that have been asked on the subject and all that has been intimated it is my belief that the government is going to proceed with a hospital insurance plan. God help them if they don't. If they fail to meet this challenge we will not have a new election in Canada, we will have a revolution because the people expect that at least hospital insurance will be brought into effect in the near future.
The experience we have had in British Columbia-and I think I can add the experience in Saskatchewan-when hospital insurance was first introduced was that people who required hospital treatment over the years requested hospitalization. This involved the construction of new hospitals. The time to start is before the over-all national plan comes into effect in order to be ready to meet that situation. If a plan for the construction of hospitals were undertaken now it would greatly assist the lumbering, construction and related industries as far as employment is concerned. But in addition to that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) should take under advisement a change in government allocations for the construction of hospitals.
A very good principle was introduced, I believe in 1948, by the previous minister of national health and welfare under which a federal contribution was made toward the construction of hospitals based on a payment of $1,000 per bed for acute treatment hospitals, $1,500 per bed for chronic, convalescent and tuberculosis hospitals and $500 per bed for the erection of nurses' quarters. There has been a vast increase in the cost of construction since that time. In Vancouver the cost of construction of a hospital in 1948 was $9,000 per bed and at the present time it is $15,000 per bed but there has never been an increase in the federal grant.
We heard from the previous government about rising costs and I am sure we will hear about this from the present government. Well, as it affects you, why not recognize that it affects the provinces and municipalities as
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald well and give benefits to them such as I have outlined. The principle is still good but the payments by the federal government should be in line with the increases in construction costs presently being faced by our municipalities and provinces in the erection of much needed hospitals. I earnestly hope this matter will be thoroughly investigated and that speedy action will be taken on it by the present government.
That is all I am going to say now. There are many other things I would like to speak on but there will be opportunity to do so as the session progresses. May I conclude by just saying that as an individual I am 100 per cent behind the amendment moved by my leader. It is an amendment of principle. By this amendment we hope to draw to the attention of the government that as much as we welcome the progressive measures they have in mind we feel it imperative for the security of Canada and the prosperity of its people that they should broaden their vision and lay down policies which will be, not only a fulfilment of their campaign promises but will go a lot farther and lay an economic, a philosophic and a parliamentary basis for a real prosperity guaranteed to all Canadians for all time.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. M. T. McDonald (Hamilton South):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour and a privilege to rise in my place in this house for the first time. It is an honour because I stand here with men of the calibre of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent), the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). It was indeed a great thrill for me to have been elected on June 10 and I hope I can convey to this house the fact that I intend to represent the people of Hamilton South in no small measure. I think it is the duty of a parliamentarian to represent his people. In the past few days I have heard more speeches on history, on religion and on other things than I have ever heard before. I have learned more about the political history of Canada in five days than I have heard of constructive criticism of the speech from the throne.
I am not so naive as to pit myself against such experienced veterans as the former minister of agriculture, but I do recall reading that it was the hydro electric system of Ontario and New York state which prodded the Liberal regime to immediate development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I should like to take this opportunity to commend my room mate, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), on the wonderful speech he made in moving the address
272	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald in reply to the speech from the throne, and with a little practice I hope that I may be able to give the same type of oration as he gave.
As a young man looking forward to a great future in Canada I want my children to have all the benefits of the resources and of all the facilities available. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) took a great deal of pride in telling this house about the wonderful immigration policies of the Liberal party. I believe that in the next 25 to 35 years Canada should have a very large population to cope with the economic developments of this country. We should have an immigration policy based on that fact, and we should tell the people in the countries of Europe and in Great Britain that it is not a picnic over here; that this is a place where they must strive to make their living.
I come from Hamilton South where we have a great cross section of peoples from all over the world, Scots, Irish, English; from Italy, Yugoslavia, Serbia and from all over western and central Europe; with language difficulties, which we have heard talked about here, far surpassing the difficulties between the French and the English. They come from countries operating under the suppression of Russian dictatorial masters. I hope that we can have more constructive criticism in this house than that which was put forth by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I am not trying to criticize in any way the manner in which he put forth his suggestions, but I believe and hope that everyone here has high ideals and a high regard for this House of Commons which holds the traditions and the heritage of the Canadian people.
As a young man watching the course of Canadian politics, whether it be Liberal or Conservative, I do not want to see or hear ever again-and I am not saying this in a very jovial kind of way-the petty and stupid politics played by any member in this house, whether he be on our side or on the other side, with regard to religion or classes. Where can a young man turn for another example than to the senior members of this house. I hope that we shall all do our duty to the best of our ability.
The riding of Hamilton South consists of a population which is half residential and the other half industrial, with innumerable small businesses, along with large steel companies, rubber corporations, textile mills and the house-building industry. They are looking for a new deal and I think they are going to get it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate you and the Deputy Speaker on your high appointments. I feel sure that you are both fine and honourable men and will conduct the affairs of the house in keeping with the British parliamentary system. I want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on his selection of the two members who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think they both did well although I do not think they can expect me to agree with them fully. Nevertheless they expressed their views and their views, taken with the views of all other members of the house, go to help to create good government for the people of Canada.
I listened with great interest to the speaker who has just taken his seat. I do not want to deal today with anything mentioned in the speech from the throne. I want to take up the effect the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway may have upon our district, particularly the Welland canal district, Hamilton and Toronto. The hon. member said that he is free to bring up matters in caucus and I would be very glad to have him raise this one there.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority and its counterpart in the United States have held hearings in preparation for an agreement for the imposition of tolls on vessels and cargos that will be using the St. Lawrence seaway when completed and the Welland ship canal.

The Address-Mr. McMillan
Many will argue that the users should pay for the canal in full. As the member for Welland I would agree to this proposition if there was any economy added to the operation of our plants by virtue of deepening the Welland canal. On account of an unfair toll system being applied I do not want to see any plants closed down or their operations curtailed. This would mean unemployment. If the price of skelp, for instance, from the Steel Company of Canada at Hamilton should be increased until it is too high in price to the tube mills in Welland it could be that the United States would supply more of our Canadian pipe requirements and thus cause unemployment in the tube mills as well as in the steel mill at Hamilton.
In any case I think the Welland canal should not be put in the same category as the St. Lawrence seaway itself. The Canadian government did not impose tolls after rebuilding and enlarging it. The canal was conceived in order to have a more closely knit Canadian economy. The maritimes now ship paper and some other products through the Welland ship canal. The other day in Hamilton, according to the press, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) said that Nova Scotia coal would compete with United States coal and be used in Hamilton. I sincerely hope that he is right. I wonder, however, if when he made that statement he gave consideration to the fact that Pennsylvania coal could be railed to nearby Rochester and shipped to all Canadian ports on lake Ontario, including Hamilton, without paying any toll whatsoever.
There are so many problems in connection with the application of tolls that I feel that this government will have to be extremely careful in setting up toll charges that they do not dislocate any part of our economy and make ourselves even less of a factor in the processing of our own raw materials.
The one big danger of setting tolls too high is that the seaway canal system might price itself out of the market against competitive carrier systems in eastern United States so far as our iron ore from Seven Islands and Labrador is concerned. As Canadians we would not be concerned if tolls were free and this ore went by another route because then we would have fewer local problems with canal traffic. However, if this happened with the proposed system- that is the system of tollage that we are about to set up-we would fail to collect canal tollage on a good or major part of our own iron ore destined for United States steel centres. In my opinion our ore should help to pay for the canals. If it does not assume a large share of canal costs, then our wheat,

our pulpwood and other commodities will have to pay more per ton to go through the canals in order to meet the yearly amortization costs.
As a private member I should like to make some suggestions for the consideration of this government. I suggest that tolls be delayed until the larger seaway tonnages are established, and I do not think the seaway tonnages can be established until the deepening of the upper lake channel starting at the Detroit river and all the way up to lake Superior is completed. At least they cannot be established fully.
My second suggestion is that consideration be given to plants already established on our great lakes system whose raw or finished products or both are caught in the tollage areas. Few United States plants are so unfavourably situated; and if they are, they have competitive routes, since the cost of the deepening of the Detroit, the St. Clair and the St. Mary's rivers is not to be charged directly against shipping. I also suggest that in the transition period smaller canal freighters be given special consideration until an opportunity is given for the building of larger freighters and that consideration be continued to be given to the smaller freighters because of the difficulty or impossibility of using larger ones at the source of raw materials.
The amortization costs are made up of the cost of the seaway plus interest plus operational charges. This will amount to a large sum of money every year. It is my honest opinion, having in mind the increased cost of the seaway over the estimated cost, that shipping cannot stand this in full. For instance, there are about 23 million tons going through the seaway. It would take $28 million or close to that figure to pay those charges. That would be well over a dollar a ton. Of course I realize that the shipping through this canal will greatly increase and thus will bring down these charges. On the other hand, I do not think anyone knows what is the physical capacity of the Welland and the seaway canals.
As one measure of relief why should not the governments themselves operate and maintain the canals as our government has done for the last 50 years? If our government does not continue to assume this obligation it will be saving a good deal of money over what is now being spent on the canals.
One good argument in favour of both governments assuming some of the costs of these canals is that it was argued here in this House and in the United States that these canals were required for the defence of both our countries and certainly that would have very little to do with shipping.

One last suggestion is that the Welland canal should continue with the charges as now paid for the passage of ships. After all its deepening will cost only about one-twelfth of the cost of the deepening of the upper lake channels. I realize that as canal traffic increases certainly the per-ton costs will come down. I hope that rates will be worked out to agree with the terms laid down by the United States congress in which they said the rates should be fair and equitable and give due consideration to the encouragement of an increased utilization of navigational facilities.
Now the other day the hon. Minister of Transport was shown over the Welland canal by the St. Lawrence seaway authorities and my good friend the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Smith) and I were asked by the minister's office here in Ottawa to join the party.
I do not think there is anything controversial in this as the minister is not here. The officials drove the minister so fast through the area that we who were riding in other cars had no opportunity to show him some of our local problems in that area, and certainly we have some problems. We have the need of overpasses or underpasses in two or three areas on the canal and we have that old problem, the old Welland canal cleanup. There is a good deal of congestion of traffic on the highway in the Niagara peninsula crossing the Welland canal and this traffic is particularly bad in Welland, Port Colborne and on the Homer bridge on the Queen Elizabeth way near St. Catharines. The mayor of Welland was here in Ottawa and he saw the former minister of transport who directed him to take his problems to the minister of highways of Ontario, promising that if that minister would make some recommendations regarding the crossing of the canal at Welland he would be glad to recommend financial assistance from this government in Ottawa. That was before the election. I know the minister of highways for Ontario was approached and I was sorry to learn in the question period last Friday, October 18, that he had not yet approached the new Minister of Transport with regard to this matter.
It is rumoured that as soon as the St. Lawrence and the Welland canals are completed their operation will be handed over to the St. Lawrence seaway authority. In the past the canals have been run very efficiently under all governments, either under the Department of Transport or the department of railways and canals. The canals have been staffed very efficiently with men who have the know-how. To turn the operation of these canals over to an authority
The Address-Mr. Olson which would not have the same or as direct responsibility to parliament would, in my mind, be very unwise.
I would just like to make one reference to another point. When I was home last weekend I heard a good deal of talk about unemployment. I met some heads of industry who claimed that they were getting no economic directives from this government. Now I think we all remember that early in the session the former minister of trade and commerce always gave the house and the country his idea of our economic outlook. On the change of government, with the talk of free trade with Britain and so forth, I think it is up to the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) to get up and tell this house what the country, industry and the people should expect. Some heads of industry are losing confidence in this government, in fact I may say some heads of industry who supported this government are now losing confidence in it. The wholesalers are not building up inventories and I think this tends to cause unemployment.
I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce during a television interview when he was in London speaking about the sale of wheat. As far as I can remember he said the sale of wheat was a long-term view. I think I am right in repeating his words. Also he said he had seen the bankers, the buyers and the bakers. In my view he might just as well have seen the butchers and the candlestick makers, because he did not seem to sell any wheat while he was in Britain. A day or two after that I saw a dispatch from London to the effect that England had bought a large shipment of wheat from the United States. I do think the people of Canada deserve to have an economic report on our prospects of trade at this time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise in my place for the first time in this house it is with all humility that I deliver this reply to Her Majesty's speech from the throne. Before I start I would like to tell you that I have just come through a bout of flu and still have a persistent cough which is troubling me. So if I am interrupted by this cough I ask you to forgive me. I do not intend to use all of the time allotted to me because I do not believe my voice will carry me that far and of course there will be many things which I would like to discuss but, for this reason, I cannot do so.
First, and again in all humility and seriousness, allow me to congratulate the Speaker on his election to the high and exacting position as Speaker of this house. I should like also to congratulate the senior members of our Social Credit group and particularly our

The Address-Mr. Olson leader for their achievements in returning a colleague to every seat occupied by our party prior to the last election.
While it may not be customary, but because I like to give credit where credit is due, allow me to congratulate the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for the success of his party on June 10th, which I believe is largely due to his own personal effort.
Mr. Speaker, the experience I have had and the events I have witnessed here in Ottawa during the past few days are ones I shall never forget, and I would like to express my appreciation to the electors of the Medicine Hat and surrounding districts for having seen fit to send me as their representative to these history making events. My respect, my admiration and my loyalty are on an even higher plane, if that is possible, for Her Majesty and His Royal Highness now that I have come in closer contact with them. May I also extend my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the reply to the speech from the throne and to the Prime Minister for his choice.
As you will all know, I can deeply appreciate the words of the hon. member for Calgary South when he spoke of the terror and the subsequent reduction to straight fear in the hearts of new members when they are in the position in which I now find myself. I beg to advise the house that if he was gripped with these emotions then I am even more their victim not having behind me the valued and distinguished service in the provincial legislature it was his good fortune to have had.
It is also of particular interest to me that the Prime Minister has seen fit to recognize the ability of all his colleagues from Alberta, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), now our Minister of Agriculture; the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who is parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence; and the hon. member for Calgary South to whom was given the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I congratulate all of them.
Since Tuesday October 15, when the Prime Minister announced that the governor in council had established a royal commission to enquire into and make recommendations concerning energy and sources of energy, it has been difficult for me to believe that this commission could do the best job possible without a representative from the province of Alberta when we know that a large percentage of the known sources of energy such as natural gas, coal and oil are found there. Many of Canada's important rivers rise in Alberta and I do not 
think it presumptuous to suggest that possibly many of the most efficient hydro sites may be located in that province where the elevation drops sharply to the east.
Perhaps I may refer again to the words of the hon. member for Calgary South when he informed this house of the fact that the Alberta government has already assessed its resources and as a consequence was able to develop policies for conservation-and I might add utilization-which have been in the interest of the people as a whole. I quite honestly believe that even though this information may be available, a representative of the people who prepared it could make an invaluable contribution to the commission.
We in Alberta are perhaps more interested in developing the sources of energy than in ascertaining where they are. In that regard I would like to read a part of an editorial taken from The Albertan of October 16, 1957:
So far as oil and gas are concerned, there's a mountain of evidence. The Alberta conservation board, more competent and more in tune with Alberta's interests than is the Diefenbaker royal commission, has conducted several formal investigations and keeps a constant watch on all phases of the industry.
Now all that will be explored again, and not only for oil and gas but for all energy sources, coal, hydro power, atomic energy and so on.
We aren't opposed to facts being ascertained, but we suspect the purpose of this move is to becloud facts, not uncover them, and the prime fact is the need for getting on with development of Alberta's oil and gas. A commission on how to reach additional markets might have been welcomed by this province, but not one that puts an extra barrier in the way.
I do not agree with all of the opinions expressed in the editorial but the reason I read it is that it is my sincere hope that the commission will not be a barrier to the development of those resources that are already known.
I am primarily interested in my own constituency and as it is customary for a new member to talk about his constituency let me first of all say that while many of the things I will talk about may possibly be familiar to the older members there may be some of the new members who are not as well informed as to the problems, conditions, etc. in southeast Alberta as indeed I am unfamiliar with many of the constituencies in other parts of Canada.
The constituency of Medicine Hat is a large prairie area consisting of some 365 townships and the people are chiefly engaged in agriculture, growing a wide variety of foodstuffs, cereals, sugar beets and many other crops suitable to dry land and irrigated farming, and in raising livestock. There is, however, a highly important industrial centre in the city of Medicine Hat and also at Redcliff and of

course there is a concentration of industrial workers there who man the plants. One of the most serious handicaps to these industries is the extremely high cost of transportation of their products to the markets and because of this I would urge the new government to give consideration to the adjustment of the unfavourable freight rates to and from Alberta. Of course the workers in these industrial areas have many problems that are peculiar to themselves but by and large their well-being is dependent on the well-being of agriculture in the west in general.
I would also like to point out at this time that in the city of Medicine Hat we have a need for a new federal building. At the present time the offices of the various departments of the federal government are scattered all across the city and some of them, I may say, are not even located in the downtown section. The post office is virtually bursting at the seams. I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) if he would seriously consider the erection of a building in the centre of the city to house all of the offices of the federal government under one roof.
One other thing in the city of Medicine Hat which is a concern of the federal government is the airport. At the present time the facilities at the Medicine Hat airport are such that many of the aircraft the air lines are using cannot touch down there. For example, only last month when the chamber of commerce of Edmonton was going to pay us a visit they arrived in a Viscount and were required to land at Suffield some 35 miles away. We would appreciate if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) would consider enlarging our airport to accommodate this type of aircraft.
Turning back to agriculture now, Mr. Speaker, it is needless for me to say we are keenly interested in the proposal of advancing money to farmers for farm-stored grain. I will not dwell on the point which so many hon. members have ably discussed, that being the fact that the farmers are far more interested in selling their wheat and moving it into the hands and stomachs of hungry people all over the world than they are in receiving advance payments, subsidies or anything of that nature. Of course, as we do not know as yet all the details of the proposed machinery for advancing this money I will leave that for comment at a later date.
The farmers in my constituency wish to commend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) for his efforts in organizing trade delegations. We do not know as yet how much favourable effect this has had in building up markets for wheat
The Address-Mr. Olson but certainly we have something to sell and I believe some genuine salesmanship is necessary to move our wheat in this age of highly competitive international markets. I would also like to suggest that when they make up this trade delegation they put some professional salesmen on it.
There are one or two other things about cereals and cereal production which may not have received proper consideration. I have read press reports in which prominent men have indicated that the major contributing factor leading up to the present surplus of cereals is the series of big crops due to abnormal weather. There have also been suggestions that a return to normal would relieve the situation. Certainly I will have to agree with part of this opinion. However, this year, 1957, has pointed up one thing that many farmers have been coming to believe and I feel that we may as well be realistic and recognize the fact that today we can and do produce far larger yields, given the same amount of precipitation during the growing season, than we could 10 to 15 years ago.
This, of course, has been brought about by several things, more know-how, new and better methods, new and better equipment, particularly in moisture conservation from one year to the next. There are other things, too, such as new varieties of grain and many other factors. This year, for example, 15 to 20 bushel crops of wheat were not uncommon where there was but one to two inches of rainfall during the growing season. This, of course, would have been impossible 15 years ago. The significance of this development is that I now believe the dry land areas in western Canada can produce all of the domestic and export market requirements of cereal grains in the immediate future; indeed, until there is some plan put into operation whereby we can share our production with those parts of the world that cannot produce enough for themselves.
The cost of production of crops, particularly cereals, which are adapted to dry-land farming is substantially lower than on irrigated land. For this reason I think that when there are suggestions to build new irrigation projects and bring more land under the ditch there must also be serious consideration given to what the people farming this land will try to grow. The farmers in my constituency who are trying to grow dry-land crops on irrigated acres in competition with the lower cost operation of dry-land farming are the ones who are now in the most serious difficulty.
We certainly do not take the dog-in-the-manger attitude towards new development

The Address-Mr. Olson
of irrigation projects because we already have these projects in operation. We do not object to hydro development, but-and I emphasize this-two or more farmers in serious economic difficulty is a worse situation than one who is doing fairly well farming the same land.
Unless and until we can set up ways of marketing or distributing the products particularly adapted to irrigated farming, and until the acres now under the ditch are being utilized, I think we should proceed with caution with any new projects. To this end, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the new government that they seriously consider giving assistance to establishing this distributing machinery.
We know that southern Alberta now has acreage under irrigation with the capacity to produce thousands of tons of specialized crops and we also know that there are thousands of tons of products being imported from the United States, which could be grown in south Alberta, especially vegetable crops. I have several briefs prepared by an official of the provincial government and various chambers of commerce to substantiate these statements.
In viewing the whole picture of irrigation, it becomes apparent that we already have the potential productive capacity and also the markets, but there is a link missing, that of processing and distributing. The farmers cannot start growing certain crops until there is a plant to process them, and it is difficult to interest anyone in building the plants until the crops are being grown. Now I am not suggesting that the government should get into the business of processing and distributing vegetables; but I do believe they should underwrite the financing of these plants, preferably producer co-operative efforts.
The speech from the throne indicates that there will be increases in old age and other pensions. This I wholeheartedly endorse. I only hope they are large enough to compensate for the increased cost of living during the last number of years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the members of this house have been very kind and considerate to me as a new member and before sitting down I would like to make one or two observations on the debates thus far in the house. Many references have been made to what certain hon. members of the government, particularly cabinet ministers, said in the past sessions prior to the last election. This appears to me to be a kind of negative criticism which I do not believe the Canadian people will approve of. On the other hand,

some of the hon. members on the government side apparently have a chip on their shoulders, and have taken the attitude of daring the opposition parties to defeat them. They apparently feel the tide is running in favour of the Conservative party. They may do well to bear in mind what the electors did to the Liberal party last June which was contrary to all predictions.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people have sent a group of minority parties here to administer their affairs. They are looking for a high degree of statesmanship rather than political manoeuvring. Anyone, and I care not from which side of the house he comes, who attempts to manoeuvre for political advantage only, who obstructs solely to obstruct, who criticizes without a constructive thought, will have to answer to the people, and I am sure that these members will be severely rebuked by the electors.
If members of the government do not mind I would like to offer a suggestion. There is a far more effective way to deal with some of the front-benchers of the official opposition while they are jockeying for position in the race for leadership of the Liberal party and that suggestion, sir, is to kill them with kindness.
