speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate you and the Deputy Speaker on the high position that you now grace in Canada's 23rd parliament. To the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) I would just like to say a heartfelt "well done". I am quite sure that the constituencies of Calgary South and Bonaventure will be very proud of you. I think your ability in the house, your dignity and fluency will make a great contribution to this chamber and to Canada.
A great deal of verbal sparring has been going on in parliament, Mr. Speaker, since we convened about a fortnight ago, and I think this is as it should be. Parliament is a place for talk; it is a place for airing opinions, but I am not going to contribute to that verbal sparring today because I find myself in a singularly benign mood.
One reason for this is the throne speech which promises to bring about so many of those things that should have been brought about long before this. Ever since coming into the House of Commons I have worked for and raised my voice on behalf of those senior citizens in my constituency of York-Humber who have been trying to live on their old age pensions. They are a gallant, uncomplaining group of people and they have made no small contribution to the progress and prosperity of Canada today.

Rising costs of living have visited very real hardship upon these pensioners, in fact, upon all pensioners, and I do commend the government for its promise to improve the lot of the senior citizens in our community and for the promise of increased payments under the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act.
I also find myself in a happy frame of mind over the government's promise to shorten the qualifying period of residence for old age pensioners. As has been said in the house many times, to set 20 years arbitrarily as the necessary period of residence before receiving the old age pension is, it seems to me, to establish a second-class citizenship. If a man or woman meets the qualifications to become a citizen of Canada, then surely the benefits that we are able to bestow upon Canadians are theirs by right long before two decades.
Finally, there was that tantalizing little sentence in the throne speech, "Changes in certain of the taxing statutes will be submitted for your approval." I do not know just what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has in mind but I should like to say this. In Canada today there are more than 2J million persons earning less than $4,000 a year, or about 77 per cent of the taxpayers. They are the people who need and deserve some relief from taxation because as it is with pensioners on fixed incomes so it is with the lower income bracket Canadian. The increased cost of living has played havoc with his budget. Again I am speaking on behalf of a good many of my constituents in York-Humber which is a suburban riding and full of young people just starting out on their careers. They are finding the taxation burden very heavy indeed.
These are some of the things in the throne speech that have contributed to my benign mood these days. Now I come to something less tangible but equally important. This something has filled my heart and mind with a profound gratefulness for Canada and for being a Canadian. This summer I went on a sort of busman's holiday which took me behind the iron curtain into Russia. I call it a busman's holiday because I did not go in any official or even professional capacity. I was not invited to go. I simply went on my own as a tourist because I wanted to see with my own eyes that puzzling and menacing country on the other side of the iron curtain.
I went, I saw and I came home thanking God for this beautiful land of freedom, for our parliamentary system where the people choose their government and we who are given the honour to serve in parliament
The Address-Miss Aitken answer to the people, not, Mr. Speaker, to a power-hungry group of 15 people in an ivory tower called the kremlin.
Last year we of the Conservative party put up a strong fight for what we believed were the rights of parliament. We believed that parliament was being gagged by closure. We could not and did not win that good fight because there was a large parliamentary majority against us. But, Mr. Speaker, under our system of government it is not in the end parliamentary majorities that decide great or small issues, it is the people. This could not happen in Russia or in any communist country.
In the throne speech Her Majesty spoke of our parliamentary government as having been fashioned by the wisdom of many centuries. Russia's system is founded on fear. Some years ago the Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill described our parliamentary system in his own inimitable way when he said:
By trial and error and perseverance through the centuries, we have found a very good plan.
During the past fortnight we have seen how that very good plan works in response to the voice of the people. The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke of the ease and smoothness with which this change of government was accomplished. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to it also when he said that it illustrated the concept of true democracy.
My sortie behind the iron curtain, Mr. Speaker, has given me an even greater appreciation of this concept of true democracy. When the people choose to elect a new government former leaders are not purged or banished to Outer Mongolia. Fear does not burn deep into the hearts and minds of those who did the opposing. In our very good plan we move with ease and smoothness to fulfil the wishes of the people. The former opposition becomes Her Majesty's government and the former government becomes Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
I am not going to hold forth on my trip to the U.S.S.R. except to say that in that country behind the iron curtain there are none of the freedoms that we cherish. There is no freedom of speech, no freedom of the press, no freedom of privacy. I think one of the things that shocked me most in Russia was the dreadful overcrowding in housing. There is no freedom of choice. Certainly there is freedom to work. Everybody works, men and women, but they have no choice of a job. A job is allocated to them. There is no freedom of movement. Even within Russia itself the people cannot travel at will. As the Russians have told us. and it is true, there is freedom of religion, but religion is

The Address-Mr. Robichaud not a menace any longer to communism because in 30 years religion has been wiped out in Russia. Today all the young adults in that country are declared atheists.
Communism reduces people and living to the lowest denominator. It is absolutely incomprehensible to me how any Canadian with any spiritual values whatsoever can look with favour upon or even tolerate communism. It is incomprehensible to me how any Canadian labour union can allow communist domination within its ranks. Russian labour has none of the hard-won rights to bargain, to strike, to negotiate for higher pay and shorter hours, such as Canadian labour has.
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to say these few words, and in conclusion I say to every member in this house, let us guard well the very good plan that our forefathers have evolved through the centuries by trial, error and perseverance.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, before proceeding with my remarks on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I should like to join with those who preceded me in this debate in offering you my most sincere congratulations on having been elected to the chairmanship of the committees of this house.
And through you, also, I would like to offer my most sincere and heartfelt congratulations to Mr. Speaker on his appointment. I am sure that he will at all times uphold the finest traditions of democracy and of the British parliamentary system.
I would also like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply, who have both acquitted themselves of their task, in a masterful way, a fact which reflects credit on their respective constituencies.
I would deserve censure, Mr. Speaker, if I were not to recall briefly the memorable moments we have all lived through during the solemn ceremonies which took place on the opening of this session. Through her presence, Her Majesty has most assuredly imparted to the opening ceremonies a character as yet unique in all Canadian history.
As a result, the colourful ceremonial and ritual observed on the opening of a new session of parliament will become better known and better appreciated. As for those of us who are of French-Canadian or Acadian descent, that is of French origin, we have been deeply moved by the words spoken by Her Majesty in our native tongue.
True, Her Majesty had a right to expect the Canadian people to express their feelings towards her as they did, but we must also

recognize that the grace, charm and ease with which Her Majesty the Queen addressed us in the two official languages of this country should be such as to provoke some soulsearching on the part of those sitting on the other side of this house who unfortunately are far too prone to neglect those principles of national unity so essential to the progress and advancement of the Canadian nation.
(Text):
In the few minutes at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with the contents of the speech from the throne. If we are to judge from certain press reports the present government, perhaps I should say the members of the present government, are very sensitive to criticism. For instance, in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, October 19, we read the following:
Conservative members in and out of Commons are talking about the possibility of a snap election unless cutting attacks which have been followed by the all-but-unanimous vote in favour of the government are toned down.
Here we are in the House of Commons, facing a government which pretends to be not quite immune to attack and criticism. I am not at all surprised at the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) announcement that a bill will be introduced at this session to abolish closure, a measure which is so commonly used in the British parliament. Is it possible that the present government, not satisfied with the criticism offered by Her Majesty's official opposition and not being in a position to apply this parliamentary procedure which is so essential to the protection of the will of the majority will counter-attack by saying, "If you do not stop or cut down your attacks we will dissolve parliament and call an immediate election." What a situation to exist in a progressive country like Canada, a country which so proudly pretends to be an example of freedom and democracy.
Mr. Speaker, as long as I am sitting in this chamber as a member of parliament I have a duty to my constituents to defend their rights and interests. It is not my intention to follow the practice of certain opposition members in the last parliament and call cabinet ministers by unparliamentary names, or to act in such an unparliamentary manner that it could result in Mr. Speaker failing to recognize me when I am asking for the floor. I do not intend to do this, Mr. Speaker, even if those unparliamentary practices of certain members met with the approval of the Prime Minister when he was acting as leader of the official opposition. It is my intention to offer constructive criticism as I feel that is the duty of the official opposition in this house.

The announcement made by the Prime Minister, as reported in the Telegraph-Journal of Friday, September 27, that Ottawa was ready to spend $3.5 million on a major harbour development at Bathurst, in my constituency, was received with great satisfaction by the entire population of Gloucester county. It is true that the project has been approved, conditional upon the New Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation Limited going ahead with plans for a further $20 million development of its property in this area. I should like to point out, however, that a decision of this kind is not taken even three or four months after a new government has taken office. A decision of this kind is too important, even for the present government, to take quickly and decisively without study. The engineers of the Department of Public Works had been carrying on experiments for the last two years to determine the possibility of such a major project. No later than April 16 last the then minister of public works, the Hon. Robert Winters, the manager of the mining company and myself visited the site of the proposed project and thoroughly discussed the possibility.
I want to commend the Prime Minister and his Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) upon their decision to proceed with this development as soon as the mining company is prepared to go ahead with its own plans for expansion. I would remind the Minister of Public Works, however, that the announcement made no mention of the public wharf to be built on the south side of the company's main wharf. The need for a suitable wharf to provide adequate shipping facilities for our local industries is urgent in the Bathurst area. Can the minister advise this house whether he has received a copy of a resolution dealing with low cost housing passed by the National Retail Lumbermen's Council of Canada at their eleventh annual meeting held at Clear Lake, Manitoba, in September of this year; and if so, what action if any has the government taken to implement the recommendations contained therein?
In his reply the minister stated that he would have to ask his department to see whether he had a copy of these recommendations. I am sure that the resolution of the National Retail Lumbermen's Council referred to in my question was of such importance to the general economy of this country, and even more so to the lumber industry, that the minister should have been
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
in a position to refresh his memory and state at once what measures, if any, had been taken by his department to implement it. I should like at this point to place on the records of the house the contents of this resolution passed by the National Retail Lumbermen's Council of Canada at their eleventh annual meeting at Clear Lake, Manitoba, on September 11, 1957:
Whereas it is recognized the low but stable income group of Canadians are increasingly dependent on their own manual efforts and private financing to provide low cost houses.
And whereas they represent a very large portion of our population.
And whereas there is a reluctance on the part of lending institutions and on the part of these citizens to assume a contract under National Housing Act regulations.
And whereas many are being forced to assume obligations beyond their means to obtain accommodation commensurate with their needs and locality.
And whereas the government should foster and assist the Canadian tradition of home ownership.
And whereas statistics indicate there is a decreasing number of people in low and middle income brackets building under present regulations.
And whereas our forefathers through their individual initiative built Canada as their funds and labour permitted.
Therefore be it resolved that the government give consideration to legislation that would permit this important group of our citizens to enjoy, in proportion to their means, the borrowing privileges now available to those in the higher income group by the following:
1.	Down payment to be considered on the basis of lot and/or foundations and owner labour.
2.	Amount of mortgage to be determined by the bare minimum living standards required by the borrower, all such building as may be done to conform to a recognized standard.
3.	Home to be completed as owners' funds permit with inspection and valuation carried out through present Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation inspectors, Veterans Land Act inspectors, mortgage and loan company inspectors, municipal building inspectors or other qualified inspectors.
4.	This would be applicable to approved serviced or unserviced rural land.
We all heard the reply given in this house on October 16 by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to a question asked by my colleague the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) and dealing with the unemployment situation in New Brunswick. One of the main causes of this approximately 100 per cent increase in the number of persons registered as unemployed in New Brunswick today, as compared with the same date last year, is the unhealthy and uncertain position of our lumber and pulp and paper industries. The average home built under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is too expensive for the majority of the average prospective home owners in Gloucester county and in many other areas of New Brunswick. A large number of families in the $50 per week bracket have been unable to build new homes which although not

The Address-Mr. Robichaud entirely up to the present Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation standards would be adequate and suitable having regard to the needs of the area without creating the possibility of additional slums which we all agree should not be incurred.
I am informed that the National Retail Lumbermen's Council has taken on its own the responsibility of building a model house which would meet the minimum standards required by this particular class of borrowers and I strongly urge the minister concerned to recommend its acceptance by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Such a move involving loans of less than $4,000 or $5,000 would stimulate home construction in many sections of the country and would give new stimulus to our seriously affected lumber industry.
One of the major problems also facing the lumber industry in the Atlantic provinces is the greatly increased cost of transportation. It would appear desirable for a manufacturer in the lumber field to have his processing plant as close as possible to the source of production or to his raw material. However, this becomes rather impractical mainly on account of heavy competition and the high cost of modern plants required to meet this competition which exists in the lumber industry as well as in other similar enterprises.
In the lumber industry, for example, it is only logical that the raw material required, which in this case is green lumber, usually sawn near the cutting area, be transported from its source of origin to the drying and planing mill. There exists, as we all know, a great difference between the weight of rough product and that of the dressed product, as well as the weight between green and air-dried lumber.
Prior to the year 1951 there existed a milling in transit privilege allowing a lumber manufacturer to bring in his lumber by rail from any point in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia on a basis of reduced rates under tariff No. CF.220-2. Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate as a newly elected member I understand there are certain courtesies which are accorded new members in that others do not interject, intervene or make any comments. I also understand that one is not generally supposed to be too harsh in his initial remarks with respect to government policy and so on. As far as I am concerned, if any hon. members feel they need to interject or offer some comments during the course of my remarks I hope they will feel free to do so.
I would like to offer my congratulations to you, sir, as other hon. members have done, in the election to the post you now hold, and also extend my congratulations to the other presiding officers of this house. I am personally very partial to the system of having what is known as a permanent speaker and I hope-and I am sure in my own mind- that your activities and interpretation of the rules of the house and your application of them will result in your being Speaker, not only for this parliament but for many parliaments to come regardless of which party might sit on your right side as the government.
However, I do not think we could quite properly apply the system which is in effect
The Address-Mr. Howard in the United Kingdom to the post you hold here in Canada. I am of the opinion that the general public enjoy having a member in this house who is vocal, one who is ready, willing and able, as the saying goes, to present the problems of his constituents, to speak in debate on the various matters afEecting people all across the nation even though they may not reside within his particular constituency. Having thought about this matter I offer as a suggestion the idea that we might approach the question of having a permanent Speaker in Canada, not along the lines of having his seat uncontested during election time but of establishing this House of Commons as an additional constituency, the members of this chamber being his constituents and accordingly electing a Speaker at each new parliament. In that way each constituency in Canada would have a member in this house who is not restricted in his speech as Mr. Speaker normally is. I do not know whether this suggestion will meet with approval on the part of the government but I hope we can approach the question in that light.
I could spend considerable time discussing the beauties and glories of the constituency of Skeena, one of the largest in Canada, but I doubt whether we should take the time of this house on that sort of thing at this particular moment. However, I might say in passing that I have a large number of 35-millimetre size coloured slides of various scenic, industrial and human interest shots taken in the riding of Skeena and if you, Mr. Speaker, or any hon. members would be interested in seeing them at any time I would be more than pleased to show you in that way some of the natural beauty of the riding I have the privilege of representing. One of the main reasons I think it is the best riding in Canada-I am sure I will find many hon. members disagreeing with me on this- naturally is that it is contained within the best province of Canada and I am sure I will find less hon. members disagreeing with me on that point than on the other.
Seriously though, Mr. Speaker, the constituents in Skeena have many problems which are similar to those which have already been mentioned in this house by other hon. members from all across the nation. I think I will have an opportunity of presenting those problems and grievances in some other proceedings before this house and I would rather leave them until that particular time presents itself.
There are, however, a couple of matters with which I should like to deal and with which other members have dealt, relating to other parts of the country. So far I have

The Address-Mr. Howard enjoyed very much listening to other hon. members relating matters affecting their particular part of the country. I was particularly interested in the question of unemployment, with which I should like to deal to some extent, not only because it affects us particularly in northern British Columbia but because it affects people all across this nation.
The most interesting discussion I have heard so far, sir, relating to unemployment, are the proposals and the criticisms advanced by the hon. members who happen to sit in the official opposition. I have noticed also that they are attempting to pass themselves off at this time as champions of practically all causes in Canada, hoping thereby, of course, to curry some favours in various sections at the next election, whenever that might be held. But personally I do not look too kindly upon their attitude now with respect to unemployment, particularly in view of the callous attitude they had while they were in office with regard to the unemployed and industries closing and laying people off. I know the individual members certainly may be sincere in their desire to overcome this problem of people being unemployed and out of work and not having the wherewithal to provide the food, clothing and shelter necessary for themselves and their families. I wonder whether this is an approach that we can expect the general public of Canada to agree with, especially in as much as those hon. gentlemen belong to the Liberal party.
We hear, of course, that unemployment in Canada and in certain parts of it has become a problem only since June 10, or a little bit later on, probably when this government took office. For the benefit of the hon. members and others who might be interested and who will have an opportunity to look at these things, may I say there are a few figures that I should like to put on the record with respect to unemployment this year and last year. To do that I must go back to the first of the year when our friends the Liberals were in office * in this country. I will not bore the house with reciting facts and figures attempting to show the difference; I will merely relate to the house the percentage of one month over the other as it applied all across Canada during the early months of this particular year. Incidentally, these are unemployment insurance commission figures.
In January of this year we had a 12 per cent increase in unemployed workers in Canada over January, 1956. In February the situation was quite a bit better than that in that the figure was 10 per cent; but there 

the good picture ends. In March we see a difference of 11 per cent; April, 17 per cent; May, 32 per cent; June, the middle of the year when unemployment is supposed to be at its peak, the election month, we find a 40 per cent increase in unemployment this year over last year. I hope the citizens across the nation will take cognizance of these figures and will look at the record of the party that was in office at that time when these things existed.
The picture, as it relates to British Columbia-and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) also mentioned this today [DOT]-is as follows. British Columbia appears to be the hardest hit of any of the provinces in the nation today in regard to over-unemployment. We find a similar set of percentage figures. They are similar in that there are more unemployed every month this year than there were last year. The percentage figures are high and I should like to relate them to the house.
In January this year there was a 35 per cent increase in unemployment in British Columbia over the year before. In February the figure was 32 per cent; in March, 23 per cent; in April, 39 per cent; in May, 62 per cent; and in June, 48 per cent.
I do not want to go beyond these figures because these are the only official ones I could get to date from the Department of Labour; but from information given to this house by the Minister of Labour in reply to questions we can see the situation has not bettered itself in the last few months in that unemployment is steadily on the increase, with a much greater percentage in each month this year over the * same month last year.
If we look at individual communities we find substantially the same picture; therefore, it is not a localized question; it is not the result of some peculiarities of an industry, be it over-production, bad weather, or some other reason. It is a general nationwide problem and the Liberals must stand up and take the proper amount of blame that they should take for having been in office during the time that this sad thing was developing. My hon. friends opposite can pound their desks because they in turn should be subjected to the same sort of criticism. Actually they are no better than the other people were when it comes to this question. Both of the parties, the one representing the government and the other representing the official opposition-incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I enjoy that expression "official opposition"; it makes us in this corner feel just that much more sure of ourselves as being the real opposition in the

house-say that this is so; I am not telling you anything that they do not agree with themselves. They agree that our present capitalist system is the one which must carry on and the only one with which they will have anything to do. So long as both parties take that attitude, so long as they refuse anything in the nature of public direction, anything in the nature of public ownership of the proper means of production and distribution, so long shall we have unemployment along with it because they know as well as I do that industry will operate and will build up the productive means of their plants if it is profitable to do so. If it does not become profitable or things become a little bit difficult the next thing they will do is to cut back their production, lay off their employees and then unemployment develops. This is a cyclical thing and it happens time after time and has been going on continuously throughout the tenure of office of the last government. Unless this government changes its attitude and is willing to take these other factors into account and do something concrete and constructive about it they will have to suffer the consequences.
I see some hon. members over here wish to say something. I am sorry I cannot hear them and am not able to make the proper comment.

Well, quite seriously, Mr. Speaker, the question of the steadily increasing number of unemployed in Canada is the one thing facing not only the government but every hon. member in this house and to which we must all put our best effort in order to find a solution immediately, not next spring or next summer or at some other time but right now when the crisis is imminent. There is every indication that our army of unemployed will reach a figure of three-quarters of a million this coming winter and it would not surprise me one bit if this turned out to be so. There is every indication that we are heading in that direction.
But the situation of people being unemployed is not the only thing that is bad. Of course some people will say that these unemployed are able to get unemployment insurance; some of them are and that helps to tide them over somewhat. However, in my opinion there is one thing with regard to which we must take immediate action. I was very dismayed when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), in answer to a question the other day, replied that it was not the intention of 96698-19
The Address-Mr. Howard the government, because the present session was going to be a short one or something of that nature, to introduce amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is time that amendments were made to the Unemployment Insurance Act. If we are not going to take action now along concrete, economic lines to deal with the problem, then let us take action along the other line and assist the unemployment insurance commission in whatever way we can in order to make things a little bit easier.
If I am not mistaken the minister was a member of a house committee that dealt with the Unemployment Insurance Act a few years ago and made amendments to it. Therefore he is probably far more familiar with the matter to which I wish to refer than I am. There is a particular section of the Unemployment Insurance Act, section 45, subsection 2, that sets up the qualifications a person must meet before he is eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. One of those qualifications is that if a person has a previous benefit year, that is if he has applied for unemployment insurance before, then in the case of a subsequent claim he must have 24 weeks of benefit contributions to the fund in that 52-week period before he can qualify.
I am thinking specifically now of the lumber and logging industries of the west coast of British Columbia which have been in the doldrums for some time so far as employment is concerned. Under that particular section the result will be that this coming winter there are going to be many hundreds of loggers on the west coast of British Columbia who are not going to qualify under the 24-week contribution provision because they will not have had 24 weeks of employment throughout the year. Many of them are already unemployed.
From talking with the president of district council No. 1 of the international woodworkers of America, who keeps a very close watch on the situation in British Columbia and Alberta, I understand that there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of 4,000 loggers unemployed at the present time which is far in excess of the normal figure for this time of the year. These unemployed people are going to have a pretty difficult time this winter to try to qualify under that particular section of the act. I hope the minister and the government will reconsider the matter of introducing amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act at this fall session in order to help to alleviate the economic picture of these unemployed workers. I do not think it would take a great deal of study to draft an appropriate amendment or even to guess at what the effect would be on the unemployment insurance

The Address-Mr. Howard fund which stands at $800 million or $900 million at the moment. It would merely mean reducing the 24-week period to some smaller number of weeks, 20 or 18, and I am sure such a move would mean that a great many more loggers could qualify than is the case at the present time.
With respect to disqualification you may think I am talking about figures for the sake of talking, but from statistics compiled by the unemployment insurance commission I find that in the first six months of this year, January to June, 275,000 people who became unemployed and applied for unemployment insurance benefits were disqualified because they could not meet the benefit contribution qualification. The figure of 275,000 does not include people who quit their jobs or were fired or left for some reason for which they might legitimately be disqualified under the act, but people who could not meet the minimum benefit contribution requirement. There were 275,000 disqualified during the first six months of the year and the situation is not going to get better as time goes on.
I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a little booklet with the title "Labour" in black print. I do not know how many members have received one of these but I am sure most members on the government side will have had them. I only wish to refer to it briefly. It contains what I assume you would call the election promises of the Conservatives and it deals with quite a number of subjects. I am sure hon. members opposite are familiar with the booklet. They probably held it in their hands during the election campaign, waved it around and said, "This is what we will do." I do not know whether the numerical order in which these promises appear indicates the degree of importance placed upon them but I see that the first one is "maintain full employment and the highest possible standard of living". I agree with both of these proposals because I think they are sound and I think some attempt should be made to put them into effect. However, as I said, I doubt whether it is possible if the government is going to follow the present pattern of our society.
They deal with a number of items to improve the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would not be at all upset if out of the six items with various subheadings that appear in the booklet they would select the one relating to some form of economic assistance to unemployed people this coming winter and not leave these people to wander around, as the hon. member for Vancouver East said, and have to go to the community chest or


other organizations of that nature to get a hand-out to tide them over for a day or two and then have to wonder what is going to happen to them.
While we are on the question of employment and unemployment I should like to refer to the recent action of the government in releasing an additional $150 million from the consolidated revenue fund into the economy of the country for home building purposes. I understand that depletes the statutory limit of money which the government is able to transfer or give to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I certainly welcome this action. To some limited degree it will help people to buy their own homes and also stimulate employment in the case of those who build the homes and supply the raw materials that go into them.
I know the government is quite proud of its action in releasing that amount of money to the general public for the great purpose of building homes but I do not know whether they should be as proud as they are when there is additional action that can be taken with respect to unemployment and also stimulation of the lumber industry which finds itself in an upset condition in central Canada and it is also pretty sick in British Columbia. Not only can the government do something by way of stimulation in that regard but they can also take a concrete, definite forward step in helping people to own their own homes and in making provision for low rental housing units, slum clearance and things of that nature.
What happens to the $150 million the government has decided to release? A person who wants to borrow part of it has to go to one of the loan sharks and interest hounds operating our banking system and has to pay through the nose to them to get his own money, which he paid in taxes in the first place, in order to buy a home, and for which he has to pay the exorbitantly high rate of 6 per cent interest.
We are also paying fees to these banks out of the public treasury for administering the loans. We are paying money to the banks for lending money to people who paid it into the public treasury in the form of taxes. Now, a much more sensible way of doing it, and a much less costly way to the person who is building a home, would be for this government to take immediate steps to arrange for that money to be lent directly through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and not at the same interest rate that would be paid to a bank, 6 per cent, but at an interest rate that would be acceptable. Perhaps the interest rate could be sufficient merely to cover the cost of administering the

loan and the administration costs of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As the situation is now with this 6 per cent interest rate or 5J or per cent, I do not care what it is, all we are doing is placing an additional burden on the person who wants to build a home. We can assist him immensely by cutting that interest rate in half. This will enable him to get a better home at less cost. This could be done in addition to all the other good things that can be done under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
At the outset I only wished to mention these two problems, one being unemployment as is evidenced by the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. group. I think unemployment is the most important question facing the people across the country today. It is true that cash advances to farmers on farm-stored grain will be of great assistance to them, but that is something that is limited to a particular area of Canada. It is true that an increase in the payments to old age pensioners, as well as the recipients of other pensions, will help in so far as the inflationary problem is of concern to them. It will help them to get along a little better in life. However, I felt that unemployment was the one question that faced everybody, in all walks of life, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It is a problem about which our government has not indicated they are going to do anything except make this $150 million available, which is a mere drop in the bucket.
They have indicated also they have asked the national employment service to step up their program of finding jobs for people who become unemployed, but that is going to be rather difficult to do if there are no jobs available. Then mention was made of programming federal works so that more would be done during the winter. I mentioned this problem of unemployment because I thought it was so important. Housing is equally important and is connected with unemployment and with the economy of the lumber industry itself. I give you these two thoughts, and I want to thank you for your attention. I hope I shall have the opportunity later of participating in debates on specific matters relating to my constituency.

The riding which I have the honour to represent is the second most populous electoral district in the nation, with a total population of 130,000 men, women and children and 75,000 electors. The constituency of York Centre lies immediately north of that much maligned, but nevertheless great city of Toronto. In fact many of our people journey south each day to their work in that city. York Centre has a character of its own. It is probably the best example in the country of that kind of community which has been called suburbia. Into the township of North York, most of which lies in York Centre, 100,000 people have moved during the past five years. As I drive through this riding on these fall weekends and talk to the members of these young families who are working so hard to maintain their homes and provide all they can for their children I am deeply conscious of the responsibilities I have as their representative in parliament.
While many immigrants have settled in York Centre, most of our young families have come from the city or the farm. We have representatives of every major ethnic group. I have the honour of representing many thousands of people of the Jewish community. In the past four years six new synagogues have been built in the riding and a new Jewish home and hospital for the aged, which is considered by qualified social workers to be the finest institution of its kind on the continent. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that a civilization may well be measured by the concern it shows for its elder citizens. In building a home for the aged and Baycrest hospital the Jewish people in metropolitan Toronto have shown not only concern but a high sense of responsibility to their community.
I should like also to express my esteem for the large numbers of people from Italy who have come to my riding in recent years. As businessmen and artisans they have had a share in the commercial and housing developments which have taken place in York Centre.

May I now bring to the attention of the house certain matters which I believe to be of importance, not only to my constituents but to those of all other hon. members. Occupied as we are with the problems of these days, it is easy for us to forget that only 13 years ago tens of thousands of young Canadians were engaged in the utterly unproductive and wasteful activities of war and that many thousands lost their lives in the service of their country. It is our solemn obligation to make every

possible effort to ensure that that kind of thing will not happen again in our time.
I hope that our government will attract skilful and dedicated people to the cause of scientific research so that our country with its immense resources may be prepared to participate in a significant way in resisting an attack from the other side of the world.
It is even more important, Mr. Speaker, that we should accept a greater responsibility for assisting the under-developed countries of the world and for helping in the reestablishment of refugees. One cannot read the report of the United Nations high commissioner for refugees without thinking that this country has yet to make any real sacrifice to alleviate the distress of these homeless people.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express the regard which I think is held by all the young members of our group for the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) each of whom has brought honour to Canada by service rendered to the world at the United Nations. It is impossible to calculate the effect of what they have done, but Canadians everywhere should be grateful to them.
I come now to the matter of dominion-provincial-municipal relationships in the field of taxation. In the riding of York Centre, the small home owner has reached the limit of his capacity to pay municipal taxes, and yet local councils are faced with the need to find more and more revenue with which to provide services not properly chargeable to owners of real property. Those who have been associated with these councils and boards of education have a great interest in the meetings of the dominion-provincial conference to be held here at the end of next month. So also do our constituents, especially those in these suburban communities where municipal taxation has become so severe.
Mr. Speaker, on taking my seat here the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) presented me with a statement made by Edmund Burke to the electors of Bristol in November, 1774. It is as follows:
It ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence and the most unreserved communication with his constituents. Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention.
It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures, his satisfactions, to theirs; and above all, ever, and in all cases, to prefer their interests to his own. Nevertheless, your representative owes you not his industry only, but his judgment, and he betrays instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
This statement, Mr. Speaker, is one which I intend to keep before me as a reminder of

my responsibilities here. These are important days for Canada, days of great opportunity for us who have been sent here to conduct the business of the country. To the members of this house and to the electors of York Centre I pledge my very best efforts as a member of this twenty-third parliament.
I shall vote in favour of the motion before this house.

I should like at this point to make a few comments on some disquieting contradictions of the speech from the throne.

The Prime Minister stated many times during the electoral campaign and the last session of parliament that there was need for "a return to the spirit of confederation". This statement, which sounded impressive, and implied that there had been a deviation from the spirit of the fathers of confederation, might suggest to many people that it was a matter of safeguarding the autonomy of the provinces.
I do not know whether the Prime Minister made the statement intentionally or not, but any one who has given the instrument of confederation some little study will admit, -and that I believe is the opinion of every jurist without exception,- that this constitutional document of 1867, in spirit as well as in letter, had markedly centralizing tendencies. It is therefore somewhat ironical to hear the Prime Minister talk about a return to the spirit of confederation while, in the same breath, he speaks of provincial autonomy.
The former prime minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had well understood that this document needed amending and had to be adapted to present conditions. In fact in 1949 he suggested certain new procedures for amending the constitution, which were to be acceptable to the provinces. Unfortunately these could not be accepted by the provinces because of lack of understanding among them. The only deviations from the spirit of confederation were made from time to time by judicial decision. That is to say that when we hear the Prime Minister talk of a return to the spirit of confederation, I wonder whether he is not thinking of even greater centralization of the economy of this country into the hands of the federal government. Whatever the case may be, Mr. Speaker, whatever his intention, the fact remains that the speech from the throne in its present state represents a real move towards centralization. I hope I may be allowed to dwell on this point for a few moments.
It will be remembered-and it is well that we should remind ourselves of these things- that the Hon. Mr. Duplessis, premier of Quebec, adopted an autonomous attitude during the federal-provincial conference of 1945. Mr. Speaker, I believe that there was fairly general approval of the proposals contained in the speech from the throne regarding our senior citizens, war veterans allowances and certain aspects of agriculture. However, on account of the vagueness of those proposals I will wait until the legislation is brought down before I refer to them further.
We in this group were sorry to note that there was no mention in the speech from the throne with regard to the tight money policy that is slowing down the Canadian economy,

The Address-Mr. Quelch and it is for that reason that the leader of this group, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), moved an amendment.
This afternoon the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), the former minister of agriculture, was somewhat critical of the
C.C.F. group and our group for moving an amendment and a subamendment. He stated that we had promised to support government legislation but, of course, we did not make any such sweeping promise. We stated that we would support government legislation that was in the national interest even though it did not go as far as we would like to see it go but that we would certainly still feel justified in moving amendments where we thought legislation was of an undesirable character or where there had been any serious omissions. Not only would we feel justified but we would feel it a duty and a responsibility to move amendments in that case.
The amendment moved by the leader of this group reads:
That all the words in the amendment after the word "once" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"However, we regret that there is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that it is the government's intention to ask parliament to lay down a scientific, modern financial policy for Canada that will guide the Bank of Canada in its operations, bring about a speedy end to the present tight money policy, and effectively check the ever-rising cost of living."
It will be recalled that the former government during previous sessions and during the election campaign stated that things had never been so good. Since that time the people have spoken and I think they spoke in such a way as to make it clear to the former government that they were not in agreement with that slogan. They showed their disapproval by the way they voted.
It is true that during the past six years there was a fairly general level of prosperity but there were danger signals evident in the year 1955. By then the cost of living had started to rise. We had an adverse balance of trade of around $800 million with the United States and $427 million with the world at large. The amount of consumer debt had risen to the figure of $2.2 billion and agriculture had become quite seriously depressed.
The governor of the Bank of Canada met with the chartered banks in the fall of 1955 and laid down the foundation for the tight money policy that has been in operation for the past two years. In laying down that policy
[Mr. Quelch.J
he justified it very largely on the ground that there was a shortage of labour. He pointed out that consequently were the money supply to be increased it would create a demand for goods that could not be satisfied due to the fact that we lacked the labour with which to expand our production. He makes that clear on page 39 of the Bank of Canada report for 1956.
Now, two years later, in the light of that situation and in the light of the situation today I think most of us would agree that the policy has been somewhat of a flop because since then there has been a steady rise in the cost of living. The adverse balance of trade which was worrying us then has pretty well doubled; consumer debt has expanded from $2.2 billion to $2.6 billion.
It may be said perhaps that one of the achievements of his policy has been the loosening up of the labour situation. At that time he said there was a shortage of labour. Very largely as the result of his financial policy we find we have many thousands of unemployed. Whether or not he would feel that is an advantage I do not know, but I think the people of this country are justified in demanding that a financial policy be instituted which makes it possible to maintain full employment in this country.
I would say that one of the direct results of the restriction of credit has been the sharp rise in interest rates, and that has forced up costs and forced up prices. High interest rates have encouraged foreign investment in this country. I know it is argued that we need a high level of foreign investment in this country in order to meet our adverse balance of trade, but let us not forget that our adverse balance of trade is actually the counterpart of foreign investment and, of course, the more money that is invested in this country the more there is spent on United States goods. Consequently, the adverse balance of trade is expanded. The practice has been accelerated as a result of United States business getting more control over our industries, and consequently buying many of their requirements in the United States instead of buying them in Canada.
In addition the tight money policy is causing our provinces and municipalities to borrow in the United States instead of borrowing in Canada, partly perhaps because they cannot borrow in Canada and partly perhaps because they can borrow money cheaper in the United States than they can in this country. The result, of course, is a steadily expanding debt between Canada and the United States.
The tight money policy is also putting the small business firms out of business and

giving the United States a stranglehold on Canadian business. I was talking to a businessman in Edmonton the other day, the manager of a firm which supplies heavy equipment for construction. He told me that many of the small business firms supplying heavy equipment were being driven out of business. He said, "We have to wait quite a while for payments from construction firms and they have to wait quite a while for payments from municipalities, provincial governments and the federal government". He said, "Normally, having to wait did not bother us at all because we were able to get a line of credit from the banks, but today that line of credit has been cut off". As a consequence, many of these small firms have already been driven into bankruptcy. What he most strongly objected to was the fact that their main competitors are larger firms with parent companies in the United States and they are able to get all the capital they want from the United States. Consequently the larger firms are taking over the Canadian firms or driving the Canadian firms out of business because the Canadian firms cannot get capital whilst their United States competitors can.
I think most of us agree that is a very undesirable situation. The other day I was told that the situation is easing; the cash reserves of the chartered banks are increasing. However, it is going to take a long time for those cash reserves to filter back to those firms who are so direly in need of an extension of credit today.
The tight money policy has also caused a high premium on the Canadian dollar. This is a very severe handicap for Canadian exporters. Years ago it used to be the practice for a nation with an adverse balance of trade to depreciate its currency in order that its exporters might be able to compete with foreign countries by underselling them. This policy would, at the same time, discourage imports. In this way it helped to ease the adverse balance of trade. But what do we find in Canada? In Canada we have a very serious adverse balance of trade, yet instead of depreciating our dollar, as has usually been the custom, we maintain the dollar at a highly appreciated rate. This results in making it very difficult for our exporters to compete with our competitors in foreign countries. At the same time we make it easier to import goods. By making it harder to export and easier to import, we are steadily widening the adverse balance of trade which is causing a great deal of concern in the country at the present time.

This policy has also severely handicapped our farmers, that is the policy of maintaining the dollar at an appreciated rate. For instance, our wheat is sold in terms of United States currency. This means that when we get paid in United States currency, instead of getting a dollar we get 96 cents. On a bushel of wheat, therefore, today the farmer loses around 7 cents as compared with what he would receive if the dollar were at par. If we compare the present situation with the situation when the dollar was held at 90 cents in terms of the United States dollar, as was the case in 1950, we find that the farmer today is losing 27 cents a bushel as a result of this highly appreciated dollar.
We in this group have always taken the stand that we should maintain foreign exchange control. We opposed the proposal to remove foreign exchange control. On the other hand, if we are not going to have foreign exchange control, if we are going to maintain the appreciated dollar, then the farmers have every right to demand that they be compensated for the penalty imposed as the result of that appreciated dollar.
I feel that parliament should make it clear to the governor of the Bank of Canada that it will not tolerate a money policy that forces us farther and farther into debt with the United States; that causes us to lose markets and, expands unemployment, and more important, places us under a severe handicap in the cold war with Russia by slowing down our production. This type of sabotage took place no later than the thirties before the world war in 1939. We suffered severely as a consequence of having allowed our production to slow down before that war. I am not suggesting the situation is similar today but I would say, in view of the fact we are entering the atomic age, the consequences might be even worse than they were in 1939. We cannot afford to slow down today whilst our competitor, in the form of Russia, is doing everything in its power to accelerate its rate of producton.
It has been stated that the tight money policy was needed to deal with inflation in this country. I think the important point to know is that there has not been any real inflation in Canada, as that condition has been defined in the past by the governor of the Bank of Canada, by our own finance officials and by former ministers of the crown. We have been told time and again that inflation means too much money chasing too few goods, yet for the past two years inventories in this country have been steadily rising while the money supply has been curtailed. I would say that what we really had in the past two years

The Address-Mr. Quelch was a wage-price spiral. Certain unions find that certain industries are making large profits and they call for an increase in wages. Then that industry increases prices, not merely sufficiently high to cover the wages but in order to give them a profit on the increased wages they are paying.
I was sorry that the proposal put forward by Walter Reuther was not given greater consideration. I thought it was an excellent proposal. The proposal to the automobile industry was that it should reduce the price of cars by $100, and in return the union would modify its proposal for an increase in wages. I should like to see the unions right across the country press the point that where there are large profits, those profits be used for the purpose of reducing prices rather than for the purpose of increasing wages because in that way they would be increasing the value of their own wages. Everybody would benefit, including the people with small fixed incomes such as those receiving old age pensions. Everybody would benefit by a reduction in price and that reduction in turn would make our prices more competitive with those in other countries and thus make it possible for us to expand our exports.
The governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Coyne, points out that consumer spending has not been a major factor in this country. I think we should note that statement because so many people seem to think that the consumers have been going on a spending spree. I note what the governor had to say at page 15 of his report for 1956:
Although certain forms of consumer expenditure financed to an increasing degree by a particular kind of credit expansion have contributed to the inflationary pressures, consumer expenditures in total have not been a major factor: consumers have not gone on a "spending spree" on the whole, and the rate of personal savings as a percentage of income has increased since the middle of 1955.
It is also interesting to note according to the October 12 edition of Saturday Night, that the managing director of the international monetary fund, speaking at the twelfth annual meeting of the world bank and international monetary fund, warned that today for trading nations deflation was a far greater danger than inflation. Perhaps I had better quote what the article said:
The other development was the backing given the fund's managing director, Mr. Jacobbson, in his contention that smaller trader nations have more to fear now from deflation than inflation-a contention that has significance for Canada. Canadians have been echoing American warnings about the dangers of inflation. Our cost of living index has continued to rise. But at the same time prices for most of our raw materials are going down and we have more unemployment than a year ago.
We hope Mr. Fleming listened carefully to what Mr. Jacobbson and his supporters had to say.

During the past six years there has been a tremendous expansion in capital investment. We have today created a tremendous productive capacity and we are in the process of turning out vast supplies of consumer goods. The greatest problem we are facing in the future is to maintain an effective demand against that production. I will agree that consumer debt today is too high. But if the total production is to be sold, and if consumer credit is to be restricted, then who is going to buy the goods that are today being bought with consumer credit? It is quite obvious that we shall be obliged to provide other sources of purchasing power by means of which to buy the total production of the country if we are going to curtail consumer credit. Otherwise goods will pile up, production will be restricted, capital investment will fall off and unemployment will steadily increase. Bankers invariably seem to be a little bit timid about a condition of full employment. They know there is a weakness in the present financial system. They know that when we have built up our productive capacity to turn out a tremendous volume of consumer goods, invariably there is difficulty in finding a market for that production. Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, in his report for 1956 refers to that situation in these words:
It is not an accident that periods of inflationary prosperity are usually followed by periods of dislocation in production and employment. One of the main purposes of efforts to contain inflation is to avoid this aftermath.
I would certainly agree that it is no accident, Mr. Speaker. It is a deliberately planned recession. It is what the bankers usually call a breathing spell. But unfortunately the unemployed are not paid during that breathing spell. Why are periods of prosperity, as pointed out by the governor of the Bank of Canada, invariably followed by dislocation and unemployment? That has invariably been the situation.
We have from time to time pointed out that the reason lies in the fact that owing to certain practices that are inherent in our present system industry is not able to maintain effective demand against its own production except in times of abnormal capital goods construction such as you have in wartime, in the development of a new country or at times when there is large scale foreign investment in the country as, for instance, we have in Canada at the present time.
We have always pointed out that that situation is largely owing to the practice of saving and the reinvestment of saving. I know that proposition is nothing new. That proposition has been propounded for many years by prominent economists such as

J. Maynard Keynes, Professor G. D. H. Cole and many others. I think perhaps it has been put most clearly by the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce in his 1952 annual report when he refers to the problem in these words:
If it is agreed that gross national production should as a minimum be sustained at present levels, then deterrents both to personal and corporate saving (investment) require immediate and careful examination. Income cannot be redistributed for consumption and at the same time invested to expand productivity without some serious strains developing-in short, deterrents to domestic investment must be examined and where consistent with domestic policies, be removed . . . Increasing consumption, both domestic and foreign, is necessary, if the heavier volume of goods and services arising out of our enlarged capacity to produce is to be absorbed.
If our objective is the optimum development of the resources of the country-and I think everybody would agree that it should be-and if a large percentage of income is to be diverted from the purchase of consumer goods to the production of more goods, then obviously purchasing power will have to be issued in order to finance the purchase of goods corresponding to the amount of purchasing power so diverted. Otherwise there is bound to be expanding consumer debt such as we have today. So when Mr. Coyne adopts a policy which is aimed at restricting credit for consumption, at the same time steps must be taken to provide for the purchase of those goods that are being bought with consumer credit. Otherwise, as I say, there is bound to be a slump, a fall-off in demand and an increase in unemployment.
In order to deal with that situation we have from time to time advocated the establishment of a national monetary commission, responsible to parliament, whose main responsibility would be to maintain the balance between the effective purchasing power of the people and the aggregate of prices of goods available for distribution. It will be their responsibility to keep a day by day check on the relationship between demand and supply. If they found that plants were running at a percentage of their capacity and if they found that demand was lagging behind supply, they would then take steps to increase the purchasing power of the people. We would suggest that the most logical way in which to do that would be to authorize a discount on the price of consumer goods so that the people's purchasing power might be equated with the aggregate of prices.
If for instance they found that demand was only 90 per cent of supply they could authorize 10 per cent discount on the sale of goods in order to equate demand with supply. Industry would sell the goods at
The Address-Mr. Quelch 90 per cent of the cost, they would turn their slips into the chartered banks and be credited with the 10 per cent and the chartered banks would then recover the amount from the national monetary authority. In that way you would help to increase the purchasing power of the people, such help being of a non-inflationary character because the increase in money supplied in that case would be used for the purpose of reducing prices rather than increasing prices.
The amount of money so issued would be just enough to equate the lag between demand and supply. Money required for that purpose would be obtained from the Bank of Canada so as not to increase the debt charges to the nation. The government would deposit nonnegotiable dominion certificates in order to receive the money. The rate of interest would be immaterial because all the profits of the Bank of Canada would go back to the government and they would therefore be receiving this money at actual cost.
I know that some will argue that if this is done you are going to expand the cash reserves of the chartered banks which will enable them in turn to expand their loans and cause inflation. That has been the argument in the past but it is not valid today because in 1954 when the Bank of Canada Act was under revision it was amended so that the Bank of Canada today has the power to alter the minimum cash ratio to be held by the chartered banks within the limits of 8 to 12 per cent of the deposit liabilities. This empowers the Bank of Canada to raise the cash reserve requirements up to 12 per cent. When this measure was before the banking and commerce committee the Social Credit party moved that the 12 per cent limitation be removed. We were supported by the C.C.F. group. We do not see any reason to have the 12 per cent limitation. The time may come when it will be desirable to raise the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks above that level to whatever level the Bank of Canada may decide is necessary.
I intend to turn now to the question of markets because we feel the only real solution to our agricultural problems is the expansion of markets. Of course there are two markets, the home market and the external market. Of the two, the home market is by far the more important for this reason: the home market has to absorb an amount of production equivalent to the total production of the country. That is to say, it has to absorb the goods left within the country and, in addition, it has to absorb the imports brought into the country in exchange for our exports. That is why we in the Social Credit group have always insisted that if we

The Address-Mr. Quelch are going to maintain full employment and maximum production in this country we have to maintain the purchasing power of the people at a level which will make it possible for them to buy the total production of the country. Otherwise goods will be left unsold, unemployment will increase and the consumer debt will steadily rise.
There is no doubt that today we have a tremendous potential market in Canada. This could be used to buy more of our agricultural products and many of the other commodities that are being piled up in the form of inventories. We have a potential market in the unemployed, the old age pensioners, the recipients of war veterans allowances and many others and we can increase our market by extending the amounts paid to those individuals and also by the establishment of a discount on prices which I have already mentioned. If we have large supplies of certain goods in Canada the discount on these goods could be increased in order to encourage their consumption. Goods in short supply could be without the discount or with a smaller discount so there would not be the same encouragement to increase the consumption of those goods in short supply.
On the question of foreign markets, we all know that we have lost many of these. We claim the reason why we have lost these markets is the slavish adherence to the principles laid down in the Bretton Woods agreement, that is to say the right of nations to receive payment in their own currencies without any obligation whatsoever to accept goods in payment.
Now if we are going to insist on payment in dollars, and refuse to balance our trade with other nations then it would make it impossible for those nations to pay for their imports from us. For that reason we have suggested time and time again that we should be willing to accept sterling from the sterling area to the degree necessary to make it possible for that area to balance its trade with us. After all, what is the purpose of international trade? Surely it should be the exchange of goods and services between nations on a basis of mutual advantage. If we agree on that basis, then when we export goods the only currency we need is the currency of the importing nations, because it is that, nation's currency which will buy that nation's goods.

I recall the former minister of trade and commerce often having argued that if we were to accept sterling we would not be in a position to spend it in a sterling area. Well fortunately many of us have had experience with sterling and have found that when we have a sterling balance in England we can use it for the purchase of goods in the sterling area and can ship them to Canada. I have done that myself. Therefore when anybody talks about not being able to use sterling balances in order to export goods to this country, they are just talking through the top of their hats; they are talking about something they do not understand.
I noticed last year that the right hon. A. B. Low, secretary of state for the board of trade in England, made that perfectly clear while he was in Canada. During an interview by the Western Producer, reported in their issue of October 11, 1956, he said that pounds sterling accepted by Canadian exporters for sales to Britain could be used for purchases of goods anywhere in the sterling area. I think therefore to the extent we have a favorable balance of trade with Britain we should be prepared to accept sterling in payment and then use our surplus for the purchase of goods from Britain. The Prime Minister has stated that he is anxious we should divert imports from the United States, such imports to be purchased from Britain. If we were willing to accept sterling we could very well use it to buy goods from Britain which we are today buying from the United States. In that way we would hope to reduce the adverse balance of trade with the United States.
